armonia-1.proposito: Mix chords from the Major mode and its Parallel Minor (for example, C Major and C Minor) to achieve emotional, cinematic transitions.

armonia-2.proposito: Map the 'bridge chords' (dominant seventh chords) that take you temporarily to any other scale degree.

armonia-3.nombre: Tritone Substitution and Altered Cadence Map (Jazz / Fusion)
armonia-3.proposito: Replace the traditional dominant chord with one a tritone away for extreme tension.
armonia-3.sensacion_emocional: Floating tension, urban mystery, technical elegance.

armonia-4.nombre: Wheel of Greek Modes and Modal Color (Fantasy & Adventure)
armonia-4.proposito: Navigate between the center (Ionian/Aeolian mode) and its brightness/darkness modulations (Lydian, Dorian, Phrygian).

armonia-5.nombre: Diminished Chord Network and Axes of Symmetry (Suspense / Horror)
armonia-5.proposito: Use diminished chords ($7^\circ$) as 'wildcards' to connect distant keys without going through the classic circle.

armonia-6.nombre: Blues Cadence Circle and Continuous Dominants (Blues / Rock)
armonia-6.proposito: Map the 12-bar structure with dominant chords that break the classic major-tonic rule.

armonia-7.proposito: Modulate quickly by dividing the octave into three equal parts, avoiding the traditional progression by fifths.
armonia-7.sensacion_emocional: Vertigo, mathematical brilliance, cascading sound, avant-garde jazz.

armonia-8.proposito: Build chords by stacking fourths instead of thirds to create suspended harmonies without an aggressive tonal center.
armonia-8.sensacion_emocional: Open space, zero gravity, meditation, modal jazz.

armonia-9.proposito: Prepare the listener for a resolution to the tonic, but divert the harmony toward unexpected chords to extend the phrase.
armonia-9.sensacion_emocional: Surprise, revelation, narrative continuation, epic pop.

armonia-10.proposito: Group the 12 tones into three functional axes (Tonic, Subdominant, Dominant) separated by minor thirds, allowing chords within the same axis to be interchanged.
armonia-10.sensacion_emocional: Geometric tension, structured dissonance, contemporary music/thriller film.

armonia-11.proposito: Create extreme chromatic tension that converges from above and below toward the dominant chord.
armonia-11.sensacion_emocional: Operatic drama, classic tragedy, imminent fate.

armonia-12.proposito: Move the exact same chord structure (e.g. Maj7 or m9) up or down the fretboard/keyboard without regard for the diatonic scale.
armonia-12.sensacion_emocional: Buoyancy, lucid dream, impressionism (Debussy style), ethereal mystery.

armonia-13.proposito: A minor progression that descends by conjunct scale degrees, creating a continuous cycle of tension that never fully resolves into peace.
armonia-13.sensacion_emocional: Earthy passion, controlled fury, desert, Spanish folklore and neoclassical rock.

armonia-14.proposito: Use augmented chords derived from the whole tone scale, eliminating any sense of tonic or leading semitone.
armonia-14.sensacion_emocional: Total disorientation, magic, alien atmosphere, transition into a dream or flashback.

armonia-15.proposito: Insert diminished chords or dominant sevenths between the main diatonic chords to create continuous walking bass lines.
armonia-15.sensacion_emocional: Constant motion, urban sophistication, fluid swing.

armonia-16.geometria: Fixed Circular Loop Over an Anchor
armonia-16.proposito: Hold a constant bass note (pedal note) while the upper-voice chords change, generating accumulating tension.
armonia-16.sensacion_emocional: Hypnosis, monstrous anticipation, trance, epic film crescendo.

armonia-17.proposito: Extend the arrival at the tonic through the use of the minor subdominant and its color variations without going through the classic dominant.

armonia-18.proposito: Keep the tonic or base chord fixed while a single inner or bass voice descends semitone by semitone.
armonia-18.sensacion_emocional: Detective mystery, elegant melancholy, spy/noir tension.

armonia-19.nombre: Royal Cadence / J-Pop Network (IV - V - iii - vi)
armonia-19.proposito: Create a sense of continuous, uninterrupted melodic motion, very popular in anime music and modern pop.
armonia-19.sensacion_emocional: Heroic nostalgia, euphoria, youthful march, constant drive.

armonia-20.proposito: Remove the third from the chord to create ambiguous harmonies that are neither major nor minor, ideal for ambient textures.

armonia-21.proposito: Structure the most commonly used progressions in commercial music (I - V - vi - IV and vi - IV - I - V).

armonia-22.proposito: Connect two distant keys using a chord common to both scales.
armonia-22.sensacion_emocional: Organic transition, change of scenery, story evolution.

armonia-23.proposito: Enrich simple progressions by adding upper layers of notes for a sophisticated, silky sound.

armonia-24.nombre: Circle of Inversions and Singable Bass Lines
armonia-24.geometria: Sine Wave Around a Central Axis
armonia-24.proposito: Connect chords not by their roots but by creating a continuous melody in the low notes using notes played on the third or fifth.
armonia-24.sensacion_emocional: Baroque fluidity, elegance, organic continuity, depth.

armonia-25.proposito: Play a major triad over a different dominant chord to generate complex jazz dissonances.
armonia-25.sensacion_emocional: Cerebral complexity, avant-garde, electric tension, virtuosity.

armonia-26.proposito: Build chords using only the notes of the major or minor pentatonic scale to avoid harmonic clashes.
armonia-26.sensacion_emocional: Futuristic brightness, electronic energy, clean euphoria.

armonia-27.proposito: Invert the polarity of harmonic relationships around a fixed axis (the C-G axis) to turn major progressions into their dark minor mirror versions.
armonia-27.sensacion_emocional: Upside-down world, familiar strangeness, psychological shadow.

armonia-28.nombre: Block / Slap Chord Diagram (Funk and Disco)
armonia-28.proposito: Move small 3- or 4-note chord blocks in syncopated rhythms with sharp, dry pauses.
armonia-28.sensacion_emocional: Groove, dancing, attitude, irresistible danceable rhythm.

armonia-29.nombre: Cluster and Microtonal Sonority Map (Horror / Thriller Film)
armonia-29.proposito: Group notes a semitone or microtone apart to create walls of sound full of dissonant dissonance.

armonia-30.nombre: Open Voicing System (Drop 2 and Drop 3 for Strings)
armonia-30.proposito: Space out the notes of a chord, leaving room in the middle so it sounds wider and clearer in orchestral arrangements.

armonia-31.nombre: Complete Parallel Modal Interchange Network (The 7 Modes in C)
armonia-31.proposito: Have direct access to the main chords of the 7 Greek modes starting from the same tonic note (C Ionian, C Dorian, C Phrygian, etc.).
armonia-31.sensacion_emocional: The full spectrum of human harmonic color, from divine light to absolute darkness.

armonia-32.nombre: Chromatic Mediants Mesh (Epic and Fantasy Film)
armonia-32.proposito: Connect chords of the same type (major or minor) separated by a major or minor third that don't belong to the same key, creating drastic cinematic turns.
armonia-32.sensacion_emocional: Awe, heroic revelation, magic, monumental scale (Hans Zimmer style).

armonia-33.proposito: Connect chords by changing only one note per step through P (Parallel), L (Leading-tone/Third), and R (Relative) transformations, with no need for dominants.
armonia-33.sensacion_emocional: Geometric fluidity, zero gravity, mathematical beauty, science-fiction film.

armonia-34.proposito: Resolve to the major tonic using the subV7 borrowed from the minor mode (bVII7) instead of the classic dominant (V7).
armonia-34.sensacion_emocional: Soft triumph, unexpected but comforting resolution, 80s pop and soul.

armonia-35.nombre: Circle of the Three Minor Shadows (Natural, Harmonic and Melodic)
armonia-35.proposito: Alternate between the variations of the minor scale to get melodic tension (Harmonic) or jazz fluidity (Melodic) within a single piece.
armonia-35.sensacion_emocional: Classic mystery, dramatic tension, technical virtuosity.

armonia-36.nombre: Hybrid Chord and Slash Chord Network (Pop Ballad / Elton John Style)
armonia-36.proposito: Keep a fixed note or a walking bass while the upper triad changes, generating chords like F/G, Eb/F, or G/C.
armonia-36.sensacion_emocional: Pop sophistication, piano emotion, warmth, TV-era nostalgia.

armonia-37.nombre: Mu Chord Map / 'Mu Major' (Steely Dan / Jazz Rock Style)
armonia-37.proposito: Add the second note (add2/add9) immediately next to the major third within the chord to create a subtle but bright dissonance.
armonia-37.sensacion_emocional: Irony, complex elegance, studio polish, 70s jazz-rock.

armonia-38.nombre: Major Subdominant Circuit in Minor Mode (Dorian Effect)
armonia-38.proposito: Introduce the major IV degree (such as D7 or D major) within a song in a minor key (like Am), raising the sixth degree of the scale.
armonia-38.sensacion_emocional: Psychedelic mystery, spatial flight, British rock (Pink Floyd / Santana style).

armonia-39.proposito: Chain multiple dominant seventh chords where each one is the V7 of the next, traveling long distances before resolving.
armonia-39.sensacion_emocional: Acceleration, relentless drive, ragtime, classic swing, comedy.

armonia-40.proposito: Renaissance and Baroque harmonic structure based on the constant alternation between the minor tonic and its relative major through the dominant.
armonia-40.sensacion_emocional: Ancient drama, aristocratic dance, solemn tension, neoclassical guitar.

armonia-41.nombre: Suspension and Inversion Diagram (4-3 and 9-8 Resolutions)
armonia-41.proposito: Delay the expected harmonic note by holding a note from the previous chord so it resolves one step later.
armonia-41.sensacion_emocional: Relief, devotion, sacred music, Baroque chorale, restrained emotion.

armonia-42.proposito: Create chords from traditional Japanese or Middle Eastern pentatonic scales to avoid standard Western sonorities.
armonia-42.sensacion_emocional: Eastern mystery, distant folklore, ancestral nature, dark meditation.

armonia-43.proposito: Design progressions where the upper melody rises while the bass descends in strictly symmetric fashion.
armonia-43.sensacion_emocional: Perfect balance, classical voice leading, choral solidity.

armonia-44.proposito: Structure the blues progression using minor seventh chords with a turnaround featuring an augmented fifth or altered ninth.
armonia-44.sensacion_emocional: Urban melancholy, lament, rain, night jazz club.

armonia-45.nombre: Augmented Chords as Wormhole Nodes (Caug / Eaug / Abaug)
armonia-45.proposito: Use the symmetry of the augmented chord (dividing the octave into 3 equal parts) to jump instantly to completely unconnected keys.
armonia-45.sensacion_emocional: Sonic teleportation, surprise, surrealism, time travel.

armonia-46.nombre: Drone and Open Fifths Network (Nordic Folk / Post-Rock)
armonia-46.geometria: Central Anchor with Long Radial Lines
armonia-46.proposito: Hold chords without a third (power chords / 5) over a rumbling low note to achieve primitive or epic sonorities without defining major/minor.
armonia-46.sensacion_emocional: Cold, Viking landscape, immensity, hypnotic weight, post-rock atmosphere.

armonia-47.proposito: Replace a main chord with its immediate scale neighbor (e.g. changing C for Dm/C or Em/C) to smooth out transitions.
armonia-47.sensacion_emocional: Extreme softness, contemplative elegance, ambient texture.

country-1.nombre: The 'Bakersfield Sound' Circle (I - IV - V7 with Twang)
country-1.proposito: Basic harmony of modern and classic country. Uses bright dominant chords to give a direct, danceable push.
country-1.sensacion_emocional: Brightness, Honky-Tonk energy, direct dancing, walking rhythm.
country-1.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Bridge-pickup use (Telecaster), pick attack with hard metal/plastic pick near the bridge.

country-2.nombre: Pedal Steel Bend Lick (Double-String Bends / Double Stops)
country-2.geometria: Parallel Vectors with a Pressure Curve
country-2.proposito: Imitate the sound of the pedal steel guitar by bending one string while keeping another fixed on its note.
country-2.sensacion_emocional: Cowboy lament, nostalgia, country sweetness, smooth transition between chords.
country-2.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Ring/middle finger bends the B string upward while the pinky holds the E string on a fixed fret.

country-3.nombre: Pentatonic Blend Matrix (Major Pentatonic + Minor Blue Note)
country-3.proposito: Combine the major pentatonic scale (sweet country sound) with the minor 3rd / chromatic b5 to give the 'spicy' sound of a country solo.
country-3.sensacion_emocional: Country flavor, mischief, fluidity, agile virtuosity.
country-3.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Fast hammer-ons moving from the minor 3rd to the major 3rd immediately.

country-4.nombre: Chicken Pickin' Mesh (Rhythm and Percussive Solos)
country-4.proposito: Create 'ghost' notes by muting the strings with the right/left hand to achieve a percussive rhythmic snap.
country-4.sensacion_emocional: Acceleration, frenetic rhythm, 'chicken-pickin'' style, rhythmic dexterity.
country-4.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Hybrid picking (pick strikes down, middle/ring finger plucks the string outward so it snaps against the frets).

country-5.nombre: Open-String Cascades / Banjo Rolls on Guitar
country-5.proposito: Use open strings as passing notes while the left hand moves along the fretboard, creating a harp- or banjo-like effect.
country-5.sensacion_emocional: Dazzling speed, crystalline fluidity, Bluegrass atmosphere.
country-5.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Continuous arpeggiated patterns (pick - middle - ring) keeping open strings tuned within the scale.

country-6.nombre: Chromatic Approach to the 3rd (The Ultimate Twang Lick)
country-6.proposito: Reach the chord's key note (the major 3rd) by sliding two chromatic notes up from below.
country-6.sensacion_emocional: Classic country soloist signature, satisfying resolution.
country-6.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Ultra-fast slide with the index or middle finger toward the tonic or 3rd.

country-7.geometria: Circle with Rearranged Sixth and Ninth Chords
country-7.proposito: Blend country rhythm with swing sophistication through 6th, 9th, and passing diminished chords.
country-7.sensacion_emocional: Danceable elegance, Texas swing, retro sophistication.

country-8.nombre: Walk-up and Walk-down Bass Lines (Bluegrass Tradition)
country-8.proposito: Connect one chord to the next through individual notes on the 5th and 6th strings before strumming.
country-8.sensacion_emocional: Rhythmic walk, clear drive, traditional folk flavor.
country-8.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Picking supported on the low strings followed by a 'boom-chick' strum.

country-9.nombre: Twin-Guitar Harmonization in Sixths (6ths Double Stops)
country-9.proposito: Play two notes a 6th apart to create a harmonized melody typical of a guitar duo.
country-9.sensacion_emocional: Two-voice singing, Tex-Mex sound, melodic sweetness.
country-9.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Pick on the low string + middle finger plucking the B string (or muting the middle G string).

country-10.nombre: Country / Americana Ballad Map (I - IVadd9 - V - vi)
country-10.geometria: Ring of Open Chords with Suspended Notes
country-10.proposito: Emotional progression for acoustic ballads with notes left ringing freely (open strings).

western-1.nombre: The 'Gothic Desert' Loop (Harmonic Minor Scale / Morricone)
western-1.geometria: Dark Circle with an Inner Spiral
western-1.proposito: Base harmony for duel sequences, suspense, or walks under the sun. Uses the major V7 in a minor key to give that 'classic', dangerous flavor.
western-1.sensacion_emocional: Imminent danger, judgment day, stifling heat, duel suspense.

western-2.nombre: Low-String Baritone Riff (Palm Muting + Spring Reverb)
western-2.geometria: Low Horizontal Line with a Watchful Pulse
western-2.proposito: Low, menacing melodic lines played on a baritone guitar or on the 5th and 6th strings in a dropped tuning (Drop D / Drop C).
western-2.sensacion_emocional: An outlaw's footsteps, latent threat, weight, funeral march.
western-2.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Dense palm muting + hard pick near the bridge + spring reverb at maximum with a touch of slow tremolo.

western-3.nombre: The Killer's Phrygian Cadence (i - bII - bIII - bII)
western-3.proposito: Generate a very dark 'Spanish/Arabic' tension typical of ambushes, moving between the root chord and its semitone above.

western-4.nombre: Gothic Slide Guitar in Open Dm (Open Dm Tuning: D-A-D-F-A-D)
western-4.proposito: Play floating, desolate melodic lines using a glass or metal slide over a minor open tuning.
western-4.sensacion_emocional: Wind through a ghost town, absolute solitude, distant lament.
western-4.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Slide with the left hand + wide vibrato at the end of each note + tape delay echo.

western-5.nombre: Shadow Arpeggio with Added Second (Dmadd9 / Amadd9)
western-5.proposito: Create acoustic-guitar or slow-pulse box harmonies where the open strings generate cold dissonances.
western-5.sensacion_emocional: Icy melancholy, past trauma, tragic tale around the campfire.
western-5.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Slow fingerpicked arpeggio, letting the E note (the added second) ring directly against the minor third.

western-6.nombre: 'Grit & Pluck' Tremolo Picking (High-Tension Lick in the Upper Register)
western-6.proposito: Play ultra-fast tremolo with the pick on the first string while varying the note within the melodic minor scale.
western-6.sensacion_emocional: Hysteria, climax of a horseback chase, madness.
western-6.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Alternate picking at maximum speed on a single string combined with a fast square-wave tremolo pedal.

western-7.nombre: Macabre Sixths in a Minor Key (Gothic Double Stops)
western-7.proposito: Play descending sixth-interval harmonies on the 1st and 3rd strings in a minor key.
western-7.sensacion_emocional: Tragic romance, funeral on the frontier, macabre beauty.
western-7.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Pluck both strings simultaneously, keeping the 2nd string muted with the edge of the finger.

western-8.nombre: 'Hunter's Tritone' Chromaticism (Using the b5 as an Anchor)
western-8.proposito: Use the diminished fifth not only as a fast passing note but as a stopping chord (power chord with b5).
western-8.sensacion_emocional: Curse, desert witchcraft, demonic or supernatural presence.

western-9.nombre: 'Pedal Point' Funeral March (Fixed Bass + Floating Chords)
western-9.geometria: Horizontal Base Wall with Falling Blocks
western-9.proposito: Keep the low D note playing rhythmically without stopping while the right hand changes small major and minor mini-triads on the upper strings.
western-9.sensacion_emocional: Inexorability, march to the gallows, relentless fatal destiny.
western-9.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Constant bass pulse in octaves while strumming or picking two-note chords on top.

western-10.nombre: 'Whammy Dip' Lick (Pitch Drop with a Vibrato Bar)
western-10.proposito: Play a minor chord or a fifth chord with soft saturation and push the vibrato bar down to intentionally detune the note.
western-10.sensacion_emocional: Mental instability, heat-induced dizziness, hallucination, hopelessness.
western-10.tecnica_o_ejecucion: Dry attack on the chord + immediate physical pressure on the Bigsby or Fender Stratocaster bar to lower the whole tuning by 1/2 or 1 step.

blues-101.proposito: Set the three-chord skeleton of the 12-bar blues in A, played with a shuffle subdivision. Lets the student hear the I-IV-V cycle bare, before adding substitutions.

blues-102.nombre: 12-Bar Blues with Quick Change (Blues in C)
blues-102.proposito: Show the variant where the IV shows up already in bar 2 and the I only returns afterward. Trains the ear to anticipate the early move to the IV.

blues-103.proposito: Work with minor blues: i and iv with a minor seventh and an altered V7 that tightens the turnaround. Useful for soloing with the natural minor and Phrygian dominant over the V.

blues-104.nombre: Jazz Blues with ii-V (Blues in F)
blues-104.proposito: Fill the 12-bar blues with ii-V chains so each dominant arrives prepared. Base for improvising with voice leading instead of the pentatonic scale alone.

blues-105.proposito: Compare three different exits for bars 11 and 12: the I-VI-II-V, the I-IV-I-V, and the chromatic descent to the V. Choose the turnaround based on how much tension you want to leave open.

blues-106.proposito: Practice the short 8-bar form, where the V shows up very early and the turnaround arrives before the ear expects it. Ideal for two-bar phrases.

blues-107.proposito: Stretch the form with four extra bars over the IV before the V, so you can develop a long melodic idea without the cycle cutting you off.

blues-108.nombre: Ninth-Chord Blues with Walking Bass (Blues in E)
blues-108.proposito: Work on slow, undulating blues with ninth chords instead of plain sevenths. The ninth softens the color and leaves room for the walking bass.

blues-109.proposito: Organize band cuts: the first bars stay silent except for the hits, and the groove returns in full upon reaching the IV. Useful for rehearsing ensemble dynamics.

blues-110.nombre: Gospel Blues with a Minor iv (Blues in F)
blues-110.proposito: Bring a church color into the blues: major chords instead of dominant sevenths, the minor iv as an emotional hinge, and a VI7 that drives the turnaround.

blues-111.nombre: Blues with Tritone Substitution (Blues in Bb)
blues-111.proposito: Replace dominants with their tritone substitute to get basses that descend by a half step. Forces you to think of the V7 and its substitute as the same function.

blues-112.nombre: Blues in Harmonic Minor (Blues in A minor)
blues-112.proposito: Use the harmonic minor so the V7 has a real major third and leading tone. The contrast between the minor iv and that dominant is the heart of the map.

blues-113.nombre: Slow Blues with Ninths and Thirteenths (Blues in C)
blues-113.proposito: Build a slow 12-bar blues where each dominant is enriched with a ninth or thirteenth, and the V arrives altered to maximize tension before the close.

blues-114.nombre: Jump Blues for a Horn Section (Blues in Bb)
blues-114.proposito: Fast blues with small big-band harmony: dominant chains and ii-Vs that give the horns something to bite into on every two-bar riff.

blues-115.nombre: Blues with Passing Diminished Chords (Blues in C)
blues-115.proposito: Insert chromatic diminished chords between the blues' scale degrees so the bass climbs by half steps instead of leaping. A classic accompaniment device for piano and guitar.

blues-116.proposito: A three-chord shuffle with a bass riff and a mix of seventh, ninth, and thirteenth over the same degree. Useful for thinking of chord color as an arranging decision.

blues-117.proposito: Sustain a funk vamp on the I and step out to the IV and the V only as much as needed. The melodic interest comes from the alterations on the central chord, not from the change.

blues-118.nombre: Bebop Blues with Harmonic Density (Blues in F)
blues-118.proposito: A 12-bar version with chord changes every two beats: a diminished chord in bar 6, chained ii-Vs, and an optional tritone substitute. It's the map for choosing a path in real time.

rock-201.proposito: Set the most widely used Mixolydian loop in rock: the major tonic with the bVII that avoids the leading tone, and the IV as a breather. Good for riffs without a classic cadence.

rock-202.nombre: Aeolian i-bVII-bVI (Minor Rock in E minor)
rock-202.proposito: Work on the Aeolian descent through whole scale degrees and decide whether to return to the i directly or pass through a borrowed V7 for a stronger close.

rock-203.nombre: Power Chords Without a Third (Riff in A)
rock-203.proposito: Think of the riff with pure fifths, where the absence of a third leaves the key ambiguous and the order of the blocks defines the character. Base for heavy distortion.

rock-204.proposito: Set the four-chord cycle that carries early rock and roll and doo-wop ballads, and see how it changes if you replace the vi with its dominant.

rock-205.nombre: Hard Rock with a Borrowed bIII (Riff in A)
rock-205.proposito: Mix the major blues-rock tonic with the bIII and bVII degrees of the natural minor. The clash between the riff's major third and the chord's bIII is the sound being sought.

rock-206.nombre: Progressive Rock in Irregular Meters (Center on D minor)
rock-206.proposito: Sustain a minor tonal center while the meter shifts from 7/8 to 5/4. The chords are chosen so every downbeat lands on a common note.

rock-207.proposito: Chain minor scale degrees with third-leaps instead of cadences, and let the bVI hang a bit too long so the resolution arrives late and dirty.

rock-208.nombre: Stoner with a Pedal Note (Riff in D)
rock-208.proposito: Keep the bass nailed to the tonic while the fifths above move chromatically. The pedal generates friction without abandoning the center.

rock-209.nombre: Punk I-IV-V at Full Speed (Progression in G)
rock-209.proposito: Reduce the harmony to three or four repeated blocks at a fast tempo, with the vi as the only shadow. Useful for working on rhythmic precision before harmonic color.

rock-210.nombre: Southern Rock with Twin Guitars (Jam in G)
rock-210.proposito: Alternate the Mixolydian color of the long jam with a minor ii seventh chord for the third harmonies. Designed for extended solos over few chords.

rock-211.nombre: Arena Rock with Suspensions (Chorus in D)
rock-211.proposito: Delay the tonic's resolution with sus4 and add9 chords so the chorus sounds huge on open strings. The sus always falls to the plain chord.

rock-212.nombre: Modal Psychedelic in Dorian (Vamp in E)
rock-212.proposito: Turn over a Dorian vamp where the major IV and the bIII with a major seventh call the tonal center into question. Ideal for drones, sitar, and unresolved solos.

pop-301.nombre: The Four Chords and Their Rotations (I-V-vi-IV)
pop-301.proposito: Show the most-used four-chord loop in pop and how its character changes depending on where you start. Useful for understanding that vi-IV-I-V, IV-I-V-vi, and I-V-vi-IV are the same circle with a different entry point.

pop-302.proposito: Set the doo-wop loop, engine of 50s ballads and half a century of pop afterward. Useful for practicing the I-vi descent and the V's final tension that pushes toward repeating.

pop-303.proposito: Work on the four-chord turn typical of Japanese pop and anime, which starts already in motion on the IV and lands on the vi. Useful for writing epic choruses without touching the tonic.

pop-304.proposito: Practice delaying the third: every chord arrives suspended and only afterward defines itself. Useful for bright pop verses where you want to avoid it feeling major or minor too fast.

pop-305.proposito: Modulate up a half step right as the chorus enters, with no transitional chord. Useful for suddenly lifting the energy once the verse has exhausted its range.

pop-306.proposito: Bring in chords borrowed from the parallel minor mode within a major pop song. Useful for darkening a chorus without changing key and for endings that sound broad and cinematic.

pop-307.proposito: Harmonize a bass line that descends by conjunct steps using inversions. Useful for piano ballads where the left hand walks and the harmony seems to move on its own.

pop-308.proposito: Play the classic pop loop with fifth chords and distortion, where drive matters more than color. Useful for fast choruses where the guitar barely changes shape.

pop-309.nombre: Synthpop with the vi as the Center
pop-309.proposito: Treat the relative minor chord as the real tonic and spin everything around it. Useful for synth tracks where you want a melancholic center that still dances.

pop-310.proposito: Build the four-bar bridge that accumulates tension before the chorus, climbing by scale degrees and braking on a suspension. Useful so the chorus's entrance feels earned.

pop-311.proposito: Use a chord that belongs to both keys as a hinge: Am is vi in C and ii in G. Useful for modulating without the seam being heard.

pop-312.proposito: Carry an entire song on a back-and-forth between two chords and save a third one just for the end of the section. Useful when the interest has to come from the melody, the rhythm, and the production.

pop-313.proposito: Jump to a major chord built on the third degree, which doesn't belong to the key and shares only one note with the tonic. Useful for opening a door of color and then returning through the vi.

soul-401.proposito: Play the basic jazz cadence with the extensions neo-soul uses: ninths on the minor, a thirteenth on the dominant, a major ninth on the tonic. Useful for making a ii-V-I sound modern instead of like an exercise.

soul-402.proposito: Sustain an indefinite groove alternating a minor ninth chord with its dominant a fourth away. Useful for jams, long intros, and anything built on the rhythm rather than on harmonic motion.

soul-403.proposito: Darken the subdominant before returning to the tonic: first major, then minor, and only then rest. Useful for hymn endings and any close that calls for gravity.

soul-404.proposito: Chain dominants that resolve into one another by fourths until reaching the tonic. Useful for gospel and soul bridges where each chord pushes relentlessly toward the next.

soul-405.proposito: Work with eleventh chords, where the fourth replaces the third and everything stays floating. Useful for mid-tempo R&B where the harmony has to sound blurry rather than goal-directed.

soul-406.proposito: Descend through major and minor ninth chords, without strong dominants, to sustain a slow tempo. Useful for soul ballads where every chord has to last two bars without getting boring.

soul-407.proposito: Use dominant ninth chords as fixed colors, with no resolving function: each one is a place to stay. Useful for horn riffs and sixteenth-note guitar strumming.

soul-408.proposito: Fill the last bars of a section to send it back to the beginning, altering the vi so it pushes harder. Useful for accompanying choir returns and organ solos.

soul-409.proposito: Stretch the two-chord plagal close into a sequence of increasingly darker subdominants before the final rest. Useful for ending a piece with four or eight bars of pure cadence.

soul-410.proposito: Roll the classic soul four-chord loop, with the ii in place of the IV so the bass walks by fourths. Useful for mid-tempo songs with a prominent bass.

soul-411.proposito: Move the same minor seventh structure across scale degrees without changing shape on the guitar or keyboard. Useful for disco and house tracks where the harmony rises and falls as a block.

soul-412.proposito: Build a slow-tempo progression where no chord is a plain triad and the dominants always arrive with a thirteenth. Useful for late-night radio soul, with saxophone and clean guitar.

soul-413.proposito: Keep the bass nailed on one note while the chords above change, written as inversions over that pedal. Useful for building tension in intros and bridges without moving the groove.

soul-414.proposito: Compare the three versions of the subdominant in the same key: major, dominant, and minor, to choose how much you want the chord to ache before the tonic. Useful for soul choruses with a bittersweet twist.

country-501.proposito: Practice the move from I to IV by filling the gap with passing bass notes, as the rhythm guitar does in bluegrass. Useful so the chord change sounds driven rather than cut off.

country-502.proposito: Set the typical honky-tonk turn where the IV arrives after the V rather than before, generating that bar-room sway. Ideal for playing over a two-beat shuffle.

country-503.nombre: Western Swing with Sixths and a Passing Diminished
country-503.proposito: Train the western swing vocabulary: a tonic with a sixth, a chromatic diminished as a hinge, and a ii-V turnaround. Useful for harmonizing melodies with a dance-orchestra flavor.

country-504.proposito: Sustain a slow ballad with the most classic turn in country songwriting: tonic, relative minor, subdominant, and dominant. Useful for long verses and narrative lyrics.

country-505.proposito: Chain dominants by fifths to build the bridge of a fast bluegrass tune. Useful for understanding how each chord prepares the next without odd scales.

country-506.proposito: Work on the Mixolydian color of country-rock, where the bVII replaces the dominant and the tension drops. Useful for verse riffs that don't want to resolve all the time.

country-507.proposito: Imitate the pedal steel effect: delay the third with a sus4 and let it fall. Useful for intros and endings where you want the chord to breathe before settling.

country-508.proposito: Keep the engine of a train beat running with a minimal sway between I and IV, using the I7 as a bluesy pivot. Useful for practicing constant strumming without losing the pulse.

country-509.nombre: Open-Chord Folk with a D Pedal
country-509.proposito: Exploit the low D string as a fixed pedal while the chords above change. Useful for folk fingerpicking and open tunings where the bass never moves.

country-510.proposito: Build the harsh mood of country in minor mode with a natural descent and a borrowed major dominant that tightens the ending. Useful for hard lyrics and mid tempos.
country-510.sensacion_emocional: Dust, grudge, a road with no return.

ambient-601.proposito: Fix an immobile bass on C and spin harmonies above it to achieve stillness with internal motion. Useful for synth beds and long transitions.

ambient-602.nombre: Chain of sus2 and sus4 Without a Third
ambient-602.proposito: Work with ambiguous harmony by removing the third from every chord, so nothing sounds clearly major or minor. Useful for pads that don't commit the melody's color.

ambient-603.proposito: Move the same maj7 structure by semitones and whole tones with no tonal function, letting color override grammar. Useful for scenes with no defined center.

ambient-604.proposito: Sustain the Lydian brightness using the major II as a permanent color over an F tonic. Useful for aerial shots, wonder, and discovery.

ambient-605.proposito: Connect major chords a third apart with a single shared note, the most direct device for a scene to change scale without formally modulating.

ambient-606.proposito: Sustain a back-and-forth between two chords for minutes and use a third chord only as an occasional detour. Useful for state-based music, not narrative music.

ambient-607.proposito: Stack fourths instead of thirds to get chords with no hierarchy, written as sus4 chords. Useful for synth textures that sound modern and neutral.

ambient-608.nombre: Whole Tones for a Dreamlike Transition
ambient-608.proposito: Use augmented and major chords a whole tone apart to erase the tonal center in a dream or fainting passage. Useful for crossing from one scene to another without a cadence.

ambient-609.proposito: Lower the same minor triad by conjunct scale degrees to produce a continuous emotional fall with no resolution. Useful for scenes of loss or wearing down.

ambient-610.nombre: Drone with Overlapping Triads on D
ambient-610.proposito: Hold an empty fifth as a drone and layer triads above it so the color changes without the background moving. Useful for long intros and sound design.

metal-701.proposito: Install the Phrygian sound with the bII a semitone from the tonic, the most economical device for something to sound dark. Useful for verse riffs and tremolo picking.

metal-702.proposito: Use the tritone leap between parallel fifths as the axis of the riff, with no thirds to soften it. Useful for drop-tuning riffs where distance matters, not function.

metal-703.proposito: Set melodic metal's most-used natural minor loop, where the bVII replaces the dominant and everything stays within the mode. Useful for epic choruses.

metal-704.proposito: Work with the Phrygian dominant mode: major tonic, flat second, and minor seventh, for riffs with an Eastern flavor and constant tension. Useful for exotic solos over a pedal.

metal-705.proposito: Rotate the same diminished chord through minor thirds to generate directionless tension, ideal for bridges and sweep passages. Useful for understanding symmetry on the fretboard.

metal-706.proposito: Sustain fifth chords for whole bars, moving them as little as possible, letting the tempo and distortion carry the weight. Useful for doom and sludge riffs.

metal-707.proposito: Lower power chords by semitone steps to create a mechanical, inevitable fall. Useful for pre-choruses and breakdowns where the harmony only has to push downward.

metal-708.proposito: Bring in the major dominant seventh within a minor context for a harder, more classical resolution than a modal one. Useful for neoclassical metal and chorus endings.

metal-709.nombre: Thrash with a Pedal on the Low String
metal-709.proposito: Alternate the fixed low note with fifths that fire off to other degrees, the rhythmic engine of thrash. Useful for galloping riffs and constant palm muting.

metal-710.nombre: Djent with Suspensions and Added Dissonances
metal-710.proposito: Combine low-octave fifths with suspended chords and clashing added notes, for rhythmic riffs in irregular meters. Useful for working with dissonant color without losing groove.

western-801.proposito: Used to build the long trot of a ride: four steps that descend on their own and never stop pushing forward. Used by repeating the cycle with a constant galloping bass and keeping the melody above in dotted quarter notes. On reaching the last step, the ride can be reined in or started over without cutting the pulse.
western-801.sensacion_emocional: Sandy, stubborn, and sweaty, with a dry urgency that doesn't rush but doesn't forgive either.

western-802.proposito: The map of the face-off: three chords staring each other down without lowering their guard, one for each gunslinger. Used by alternating the vertices over long silences, never fully resolving, to stretch the tension before the shot. The Neapolitan second degree is what raises the cold sweat.
western-802.sensacion_emocional: Still, sharp, and sweaty, like three shadows nailed to the noon sun waiting for the first blink.

western-803.proposito: A chromatic bass-line map under a chord that barely moves: the bass walks down a semitone per bar while a tremolo sits on top. Used to accompany slow walks, burials, and arrivals at the town. Each chromatic step changes the color without changing the key.
western-803.sensacion_emocional: Funereal, slippery, and heavy, like a coffin dragged down the main street.

western-804.nombre: Augmented Triads at High Noon (C / Am)
western-804.proposito: Uses augmented triads to spin with no center: each one repeats the last, shifted a major third, so the spiral never lands. Used in shots of heat, hallucination, and thirst, with tremolo guitar and whistling on top. The two natural chords at the end are the only way out to solid ground.
western-804.sensacion_emocional: Dazzling, dizzy, and reverberant, like staring at the horizon until it shimmers.

western-805.nombre: Tonic Pedal in the Ghost Town (Am)
western-805.geometria: core with a radial orbit around the pedal
western-805.proposito: The bass is nailed to the tonic and the whole harmony spins above it: the core is Am and the satellites change one voice at a time. Used to sustain scenes of an empty town, banging shutters, and long shots with no action. Always returning to the core before moving to the next satellite keeps the emptiness intact.
western-805.sensacion_emocional: Hollow, suspended, and dusty, with a stillness that scrapes like sun-dried wood.

western-806.proposito: Runs through the six most useful degrees of the harmonic minor in Gm, with the raised seventh as a permanent edge. Used when threat is needed without a quick resolution: each side of the hexagon is a legal step, and any diagonal works as an abrupt cut. The dominant with the flat ninth is the way out.
western-806.sensacion_emocional: Narrow, threatening, and metallic, like a stone echo throwing the gunshot back before it's fired.

western-807.proposito: A map of minor sixth chords, that half-diminished color that sounds like a wooden cross. Used at a slow tempo, arpeggiated, letting the sixth ring longer than feels comfortable. The rhombus's diagonals let you jump straight from rest to the dominant when the scene needs a sharp blow.
western-807.sensacion_emocional: Solemn, sour, and resigned, with the weight of a shovel that has already dug too much.

western-808.geometria: cluster cloud, with no fixed center
western-808.proposito: Every node is a suspension or an added tone that never resolves to a triad: the cloud floats and moves by proximity, not by function. Used in passages of waiting, blowing sand, and decisions never made. The rule is that no chord may fall to its obvious resolution while the map is active.
western-808.sensacion_emocional: Floating, incomplete, and parched, like a question left hanging in the hot air.

western-809.proposito: Five wide entries that narrow down until they all fall into the same dominant: the map of a closing trap. Used by accelerating the harmonic rhythm as it moves through the funnel, from four bars down to one. Nothing escapes the funnel except through the final mouth.
western-809.sensacion_emocional: Oppressive, accelerating, and inescapable, with the pulse tightening against the stone wall.

western-810.proposito: Alternates in a zig-zag between the minor axis and chords borrowed from the major, never staying twice on the same side. Used for chases where the terrain changes: each bounce of the zig-zag is a cut in the shot. The dominant always appears on the upper bounce so the hit lands off the beat.
western-810.sensacion_emocional: Pounding, jolting, and ragged, with the energy of hooves changing direction over loose gravel.

pop.resumen: Four chords you already know, with all the work put into making the melody land on the first try.

progresiones.nota: The most used progression in popular music. It works because it never quite leaves home: the vi makes you think it turned sad and the IV brings you back.
The same wheel starting on the minor. It sounds more melancholic without changing a single note.
The one from the 50s. More innocent, rounder.
Starting on the IV takes the weight off the first bar: the tonic only arrives in the second bar, so the chorus sounds like it's already in motion.
Descending bass by thirds with two minor chords in the middle. Works for bridges because it lowers the energy without changing key.
The bVII is a borrowing from mixolydian: it brings the minor seventh and removes the half step of the classic cadence, which is why it sounds flatter and more rock than a V–I.
The same four-chord loop read in minor. They're all natural degrees of aeolian, so there's no dominant and the progression spins without resolving.
The iv borrowed from the minor lowers the third of the IV by a half step, and that motion against the tonic is what produces the typical bittersweet effect at the end of the chorus.
A descending bridge by step that stalls on the V and stays there. Since it never touches the tonic, when the chorus returns on I the relief is obvious.
The II7 is the dominant of the dominant: it brings in a note foreign to the key that pushes hard toward the V. It's the shortest path to modulate to the key of the V in the final chorus.

The root descends by fifths from D to G to C, and the F–B tritone of the G7 resolves by half steps to E–C. The move to Am7 keeps three notes in common with Cmaj7, so the cycle starts again without a break.
Em shares E and G with C, so the move is almost a bass change. The step from F to Fm lowers the third A to Ab, a small half step that points straight to G or back to the E of the tonic chord.
The first two chords are minor with a descending fifth and share the note E. Then F rises to C by plagal motion, and the leading tone never appears: the color stays suspended between major and minor.

Starting on IV pushes by step up to vi, which acts as a substitute tonic. Ending on iii leaves the major third of the tonic (G) ringing in the listener's ear, so the return to I doesn't need a dominant.
D7 is a secondary dominant of G: its F# is a borrowed leading tone that resolves to G. It works to tonicize the V one bar before returning to I, without leaving the key.
Ab comes from the parallel minor and makes the bass drop A–Ab, a half step. From there Bb and C rise by whole steps, so the arrival at the tonic is by step, not by fifth.

Four chords with the bass rising by scale degrees: the tension grows only through height, without a strong change of function. It works as a pre-chorus because it leaves the V open, waiting for the I.
Modal interchange swaps A for Ab over the same F bass. That Ab then falls to G, the fifth of the tonic, and there the I arrives resolved even though there was no dominant.
Adding Bb to C turns it into the dominant of F, so the IV arrives tonicized. The Fm that follows lowers A to Ab and sets up a chromatic descent toward G or toward the tonic's E.
Three chained descending fifths, with sevenths resolving down a step at each change. The final C6 avoids full rest because the sixth A still sounds like a common note with Am7.

Starts outside the major key: the Bb brings the minor seventh and makes the whole thing a chain of ascending fifths. Since each chord is the dominant of the next by position, the drive doesn't stop until the V.
The first three chords each share two notes, so the top voice can stay put on E. The jump to V at the end introduces the leading tone B only in the last bar.
Dm and F have the same notes minus one — it's more a color change than a function change. Ending on iii keeps the G common with the tonic and leaves the phrase half-open to repeat the cycle.

Everything in natural minor until the end, where the E7 brings G# from harmonic minor. That G# sits a half step from the A of the tonic and a half step from the bass note F, so it closes by minimal voice leading.
The D7 appears right after the IV, sharing a bass note a descending fifth away (inverted). Its F# contradicts the previous F, and that chromatic clash is what pushes toward the V.

transiciones.porque: The 'amen' cadence. It resolves without the push of the V, softer and more open — which is why so many choruses end there.
You promise the tonic and land on the relative minor instead. It's the trick that keeps a chorus from ending and spinning again.
Slip an Isus4 before the IV: the fourth already hints at the note of the coming chord, and the change feels inevitable.
The ear expects the tonic and gets the relative minor instead, which shares two notes with it. It's a false close and stretches the chorus one more cycle.
They share two notes, so the change feels like a new color rather than a modulation. The bass drops a third and pulls the phrase downward.
Turning the tonic into a dominant adds the minor seventh, which sits a half step above the third of the IV and resolves there. It pushes toward the IV instead of just arriving.
The bass rises a whole step instead of a half step, so there's no dominant tension: it closes by weight, not by resolution. Sounds modern and somewhat modal.
The minor sixth of the iv drops a half step to the fifth of the tonic. It's a plagal close with a note borrowed from the minor, which is why it sounds nostalgic.
It treats the vi as a momentary tonic: the III7 is its dominant and brings the half step that confirms it. It gives the relative minor its own identity before returning to I.
Instead of resolving, it uses the dominant of the new key: the final chorus enters a whole step higher and everything sounds brighter, with more room for the voice.
The sus4 delays the third B and only lets it fall on the last beat. When the chorus comes in, the leading tone is already active and the I arrives without needing a rhythmic hit.
F and Am share A and C, so the tonal center shifts without changing the material. The G# of the E7 is the only new note and functions as the leading tone of the new center.
Bb is the bVII of the original key and the IV of the new one — a pivot chord. The bass G–Bb–A–Bb surrounds the new tonic from above and below before confirming it.
The bass descends by step G–F#–E and reaches the relative minor by step, not by leap. G and Em share G and B, so only the lowest note of the arrangement changes.
The Ab of the Fm7 falls to G, and the implied Eb of the minor color pulls toward the bass E. Arriving on I in first inversion keeps the motion going without sounding final.
The D7 tonicizes the V and announces a new section without leaving the key. Its notes F# and C form a tritone that resolves to G and B when the solo starts.
F6 brings in the sixth D, which is a common note with the following G and softens the change of function. From there the bass rises by step F–G–C and the major tonic returns without a harsh contrast.
The root stays fixed and only the top voice moves, B–A–D, within the same chord. With no change of function, the section dissolves instead of closing.
The chromatic bass D–C#–B reaches the relative minor by half step and whole step. A/C# acts as an inverted dominant of Bm, with the C# a half step from the new center.
The sevenths descend by step across three chords in a row, so the descent is linear. The final G7 reinstates the tritone and brings back the tension the verse needs to start.

licks.nota: Descends through the major pentatonic and lands on the tonic. It's the fill between two sung phrases.
A short phrase to slip between two verses: it drops from E to C on the first string and closes with a hammer-on back to the tonic. Being major pentatonic, it clashes with no chord in the key.
Rises D-E-G-A and comes back the same way: a symmetrical curve that works as an answer to a sung phrase. The hammer-on and pull-off make it sound slurred rather than picked.

licks.nombre: Ionian ascent in D toward the tonic
licks.nota: Rises by step from F# up to high D: using the full scale brings out the final C#-D half step, which is what confirms the major key.
Five notes going up and three coming down within the same box. It works as a bridge between two phrases because it starts and ends on notes of the tonic chord.

licks.nombre: Phrase in F Ionian with the fourth
licks.nota: Reaches up to high F passing through Bb, the fourth of the scale: that note brushes against the third of the tonic chord, so you have to release it quickly toward E.
Uses three strings to open up the range: rises from the E on the third string to high E and back. Moving by thirds instead of steps makes it sound singable rather than scalar.
Rises through the major pentatonic box, leaning on the thirds B and E. With no fourth or seventh, nothing clashes with the IV or the V of the progression.
Alternates fretted notes with open strings, so the pitches overlap and sound arpeggiated. It leans on E and G, the third and fifth of the tonic.
The major sixth F# is what separates this color from natural minor and appears as a passing note toward G. The minor seventh G leaves the phrase open, with no leading tone.
The minor seventh C and the major third F# form the interval that defines the dominant chord. The phrase ends on the ninth E so the resolution stays pending.
Uses first position so the open low E works as a pedal. The natural G fixes the minor third, and the D avoids any sense of a leading tone.
The pair C–C# puts the minor third right against the major third, and that half step is the whole effect. Always resolving to C# keeps the phrase sounding major.
Stays in the high strings to avoid clashing with the vocal in the middle register. The main notes are G and A, the fifth and sixth, common to both the I and the vi.

The phrase passes through F# and lands on G — a leading tone to tonic by ascending half step. Before that it leans on C and E, the fourth and sixth, the notes of the IV, which fall to the tonic chord.

rock.resumen: The bVII borrowed from mixolydian, power chords without a third, and the minor pentatonic over everything.

progresiones.nota: The mixolydian progression. That D major doesn't belong to E major: it comes from the mixolydian mode and is exactly what sounds like rock instead of pop.
The epic descent. Works as a chorus when the riff needs to open up.
The old familiar skeleton, played with power chords and distortion.
The quintessential mixolydian progression: the bVII replaces the V and keeps the major key but without the classic cadence. The tonic's minor pentatonic sits well over the top.
The first three descending degrees of aeolian and back. Since it never reaches the V, the loop holds up on its own through the weight of the bass descending by step.
Rock's most common minor loop: every chord is major except the tonic, so it sounds big and open despite being in minor.
The modal version of I-IV-V: the minor v, with no major seventh, avoids the classic cadence and keeps the dark aeolian color from start to finish.
The bIII is a borrowing from the minor pentatonic over a major key: that clash between minor and major third is the foundation of the blues-rock sound.
A riff in fifths where the bass moves by descending fourths. Being power chords, the same fingering can be moved along the neck without worrying about chord quality.
Drops to the v and then rises by step from the bVI. The final ascent builds momentum toward the tonic without using a dominant.
Andalusian descent: the first three are from aeolian and the final major chord comes from harmonic minor. That borrowed G# makes the cycle restart with force.
The sus4 suspends the third and releases it on resolution: it's a riff trick that lets the tonic move without changing chord before dropping to the bVII.

The first three chords are from natural minor with the bass descending by thirds and fourths. The final iv brings back the F, which falls a half step to the E of the tonic chord when the cycle returns.
Each chord is a fourth above the previous one, so it's really a chain of descending fifths in disguise. With no leading tone, the D acts as a temporary rest rather than a dominant.
The G contradicts the G# brought by the E major, and that half step is the pivot point of the progression. Then the D drops a fifth to the I and closes the loop without needing a dominant.
F and Dm share F and A, so the middle move is nearly static. The final E major introduces G# as a leading tone and resolves by half step to A.
The minor ii shows up where a V was expected, leaving the tension open. The C is a bVII borrowed from mixolydian and falls a whole step to the D bass when the loop returns.
The bass rises by whole steps F–G and then falls by thirds to the tonic. Since the v is minor, the arrival at i has no leading tone and sounds like a fifth descending, not an attraction.
Rises by thirds and then by fourths, covering nearly the whole natural minor scale in four steps. The D leaves the minor seventh on top and returns to i by a descending whole step.
The G clashes with the G# of the major tonic triad: that rub between minor third and major third drives the riff. Then D and A drop by fifths and pull the focus back to the I.
The E brings in G# from harmonic minor and forms an augmented second with the F of the iv. The return to i is by descending fourth and keeps the minor color intact.
C#m shares C# and E with the tonic chord, so the change is more about the bass than the harmony. The D rises to A by fourth and keeps everything within the major, with no bVII.
The bass drops E–D and keeps falling down to B, all by scale steps of the minor. The final C rises a half step to the previous inverted B and pushes back toward the i.
Without thirds, the progression is neither major nor minor, and the parallel fifths keep everything open. The C brings the interval of a minor third over the tonic purely as bass motion.
Four descending fifths in a row, so each chord sets up the next by its root. On reaching the bIII the ear takes it as a relative tonic, and the repeat reframes the Bm.
The E major brings in G#, the raised fourth of the key, which gives it that bright color. The following G restores the natural fourth, and the contrast of that half step drives the riff.
A chain of ascending fifths that reaches the tonic from below in the circle of roots. Since every chord is major, the minor seventh of the bIII only resolves at the very end.

transiciones.porque: Rises a whole step to the tonic without passing through the V. There's no leading tone, and that lack of urgency is what sounds like rock.
From E to G: it takes you into minor territory without changing the tonic. A classic for the bridge.
Goes from the V to the IV instead of resolving. It breaks the classical rule, which is exactly why it pushes forward.
The bass rises a whole step instead of a half step: it closes with weight but without tritone tension, which is exactly what separates modal rock from tonal pop.
In an aeolian progression, the major V brings the major seventh of the key, foreign to the mode. That half step resolving to the tonic makes the riff's restart feel inevitable.
Two major chords a whole step apart push toward the minor tonic purely by parallel motion. It's the most direct way to build an armonic crescendo.
They share two notes, so the change opens up the sound without modulating. It makes the chorus sound brighter than the verse.
With power chords the two voices move in parallel with no voice leading: the effect is a block sliding along the neck, characteristic of the rock riff.
The same finger shape moved five frets up keeps the riff's identity while changing the harmony. It saves you from having to think out two different figures.
The bass drops a half step and the chord shifts from modal to dominant: it's the point where an aeolian progression turns tense and demands the tonic.
Rises a fourth while keeping the mode's minor third. No new notes, so the change darkens things without leaving aeolian.
The D is the bVII of the starting key and the IV of the new one — a direct pivot. The bass drops by whole steps E–D and then rises a fourth, so the arrival has punch.
Changing C to C# turns the minor tonic into a dominant and opens the door to the major third in the solo. The following D confirms the new fourth and leaves the natural C as the seventh.
The basses rise by whole steps F–G–A with no dominant chords. The stepwise rise gives the push that a V would give here, with no leading tone appearing at all.
The thirdless fifths leave the modality undefined until the vocal enters. The bass runs through D–C–G, the roots of mixolydian, and returns to center by a descending fourth.
The bass rises chromatically E–F#–G up to the relative major. Em and G share G and B, so only the center of gravity shifts, not the notes.

The sus4 removes the third and loosens the major color before dropping to the bVII. By the time the G arrives, the section has already lost the leading tone and sounds heavier without changing the reference root.
Two major chords rising by whole steps arriving on the fifth of the tonic. The parallel motion avoids functional resolution, which is why the riff re-enters as if it never left.
The F is the bVI of the old key and the V of the new one, so it works as a pivot. Its third A is both the tonic being left behind and the leading tone of the new center.
The roots rise by whole steps up to the D, which only then behaves like a dominant. The leading tone F# appears only in that final chord and resolves by half step to G.
The root stays fixed while the inner voice drops D–C#, turning the seventh into a sixth. With no change in bass or function, the section holds until the cut.

licks.nota: The low notes of the riff: tonic, minor seventh, and fourth. With palm mute and all downstrokes.
The box at the 12th position, up and down. The bend at fret 15 goes up a whole step.

licks.nombre: Low riff in E with open string
licks.nota: Alternates the open sixth string with notes from the minor pentatonic: the open E works as a rhythmic pedal and the rest is the answer. Alternate picking with light palm mute.
Climbs the three low strings up to the G, the minor seventh, and back: that note is what defines the mixolydian color against a major scale.

licks.nombre: Bend solo in A minor pentatonic
licks.nota: Climbs the fifth-position box, and the bend on the G takes it up a whole step to the tonic: that gesture resolves the phrase without changing position.

licks.nombre: Aeolian phrase in E, twelfth position
licks.nota: Uses the full scale so the C shows up — the minor sixth, the note that distinguishes aeolian from the minor pentatonic. Ends on the tonic an octave up.
The bend on the F rises a whole step to G: it's easy to control on the second string and points the phrase at the tonic before dropping back to the box.
Works between the fourth and third strings around the C and the G: the minor seventh and the fourth give that flat, unresolved riff sound.
The minor seventh G pulls toward the A by a descending whole step, and the bend on the fifth E loads the phrase. With no second or sixth, no note interferes with the bVII or the iv.
The Bb is the raised fourth and always appears between A and B as a chromatic passing note. The resolution lands on the open E, which acts as a pedal.

licks.nombre: Mixolydian phrase over a major riff
licks.nota: The major third C# and the minor seventh G coexist, which is exactly the sustained-dominant color. The G falls a whole step to F# and from there to E, the fifth of the tonic.
The minor sixth Bb falls a half step to A, and that motion is what fixes the natural minor color. The phrase avoids the leading tone, so the bVII sounds like a rest rather than tension.
The major sixth E is what distinguishes this color from natural minor and always lands over the IV chord. The minor seventh F rises a whole step to G and closes the loop.
Combines open strings with fretted notes, so the pitches overlap and the phrase sounds continuous. It leans on G and D, the minor third and the minor seventh.
The major third F# and the sixth B give an open color with no seventh, so it works over both I and IV. The phrase ends on E, the ninth, left hanging for the riff to come in.
The Db between C and D works as a passing raised fourth, and the slide underlines that half step. The F either falls a whole step to the implied Eb or rises to G, depending on how the phrase closes.

blues.resumen: Twelve bars, three dominant chords, and a third that never decides between major and minor.

progresiones.nota: The twelve bars. What's strange and great is that the tonic is also a dominant: it never fully resolves.
The full turnaround: the last two bars bring you back to the top.
Minor blues. The same skeleton with minor chords and an altered dominant at the end.
Quick change: the IV7 shows up already in the second bar and then returns to the I7. It breaks the monotony of four identical opening bars.
The last four bars of the classic blues. The V7 going to the IV7 would be strange in tonal harmony, but here it's the style's signature; the final V7 restarts the loop.
Jazz-blues turnaround: instead of staying on the V7, it builds a chain of fourths landing on the dominant. Gives more harmonic movement to improvise over.
Minor blues: the whole cycle stays minor except for the bVI7 and V7, which drop by half step toward the tonic. That descent is what gives it the dramatic character.
Bars 9 through 12 in jazz-blues style: it resolves to the I7 and the final VI7 reopens the cycle toward the ii7, chaining dominants.
The chromatic diminished chord between the IV7 and the I7 takes advantage of sharing three notes: it raises the bass a half step and works as a bridge without changing the color.
Tritone substitution of the V7: the bII7 has the same tritone as the dominant, but the bass falls by half step to the tonic, which sounds smoother and more jazz-like.
Eight-bar blues: the dominant arrives much sooner and the cycle closes in half the time. Very common in mid-tempo sung blues.
Chain of secondary dominants: each chord is the dominant of the next. It's the ragtime device used for intros and bridges within the blues.

Sixteen-bar format: the IV7 reappears in the second phrase before the I7 asserts itself. Each I7–IV7 move shifts the seventh of the I (F) a half step to the third of the IV (E), so the fourth leap sounds chromatically led rather than forced.

The iv7 minorizes the IV, lowering its third (F# to F) a half step, which is the minor seventh of the I. That F becomes a common note with the following A7 and closes the phrase without needing a dominant.

Substitution by major thirds: each dominant resolves down a major third, chaining three centers 4 semitones apart. The dominants' sevenths drop a half step to the third of the following maj7, so the chain holds together through tritone resolution at each link.
The VI7 with b9 works as a secondary dominant of the ii: its b9 (Bb) falls to the fifth A of Dm7 and its third C# rises to the root D. Then the ordinary ii–V returns the tritone to the I.

The last bars of the slow blues descend by whole steps from the I down to the VI7 and then enter the ii–V. The #9 of the D7 is the F that had been sounding as the root of the I, so the function change is heard without moving that voice.

Minor blues with an altered dominant: the b9 (F) of the E7 is a common note with the bVImaj7 and falls to the fifth E of Am7. The bVImaj7 before the V7 provides root motion by descending half step (F to E).

Jump-blues turnaround: the sixth of the I avoids the seventh and leaves an open sound for the VI7, whose third B rises to the root C of the ii7. The V9 adds the ninth G, a common note with the previous bar's G7.

The bIII7 is a passing dominant between I and IV: its third B is the fifth of the I and its seventh F rises by half step to the root... more precisely, its root G rises a whole step to the root A of the IV. The shared third B links all three chords.
A chromatic descent of dominants toward the V. Each root falls a half step or whole step, and the sevenths trace a parallel descending line, so the tension builds without resolving until the V7.

The bII13 is the tritone substitute of the V: it shares third and seventh with the G7, inverted (F and Cb/B). Its root Db falls a half step to the final C, the most direct possible resolution to the I.
The #ivdim7 appears as a passing chord between IV and I: all four of its voices sit a half step or whole step from those of the I, with the fifth in the bass. The D# rises to E, the fifth of the I.
Gospel-blues version with the I as maj7: the vi7 shares three notes with the I and falls a third to the ii7. The 13th of the V (G) is the third of the I and is already present before the resolution.
A diatonic descent of natural minor with the degrees turned into dominants. The bVI7–V7 step moves the root by half step, and the b9 of the V (Ab) is a common note with the previous chord.

Blues over harmonic minor: the sixth of the i (F#) contrasts with the natural F of the V's b9 and generates the chromatic motion that defines the sound. The G# of the dominant rises a half step to the root of the i every time it returns.
The dim7 over #I walks the bass from I to ii by half steps and works as a rootless dominant of the ii. Its notes E, G, and Bb were already in the C7, so only the bass moves.

transiciones.porque: It's the moment where the blues 'opens up'. Anticipate it by playing the b7 of the I in the previous bar: that note already belongs to the IV.
Instead of resolving to the I, it drops to the IV. It's what stretches out the last few bars.
A diminished chord a half step up connects the I to the ii, or back to the IV, without you noticing the seam.
The minor seventh of the I7 sits a half step above the third of the IV7 and resolves there. It's the most tonal move in the blues, which is why it marks the section change.
Goes from the dominant to the subdominant, the reverse of what classical harmony calls for. Sounds like a controlled drop and sets up the arrival at the I7.
The diminished chord shares three notes with the IV7 and raises the bass a half step, so the change feels like rising tension rather than a new chord.
Turns bar 9 into a two-five: it introduces the half-step voice leading that basic blues doesn't have, opening the door to phrases with notes outside the pentatonic.
Two dominants a half step apart: the parallel descent is the most direct way to build tension in a minor blues before returning to the tonic.
The VI7 is the dominant of the ii7, so it anticipates the turnaround. It brings in a major third foreign to the key that grabs attention just before the end of the loop.
Shares the tritone with the V7, but the bass falls a half step to the tonic. Same level of tension, smoother motion.
Rising by half steps from the tonic up to the root of the IV7 fills the bar without changing chord: the tension is produced by the bass, not the harmony.

transiciones.como: Hold the F of the G7 and drop the B to Bb in the top voice.
transiciones.porque: The F is the seventh of the I and the third of the IV, so it stays put; the B falls a half step to the seventh of the IV, producing the only audible motion.

transiciones.como: Raise only the bass a half step and leave the three upper voices still.
transiciones.porque: E, G, and Bb belong to both chords; with the bass on C# the group reads as the dominant of the ii, and the motion stays in a single voice.

transiciones.como: Drop the third C# to C and raise the seventh G to A.
transiciones.porque: The C#–G tritone opens out to C–A, the seventh and fifth of Dm7; the interval resolves outward by half step and whole step.

transiciones.como: Slide the whole voicing down a half step before resolving to the I.
transiciones.porque: The Db7 is the tritone substitute of the alternate V, and its seventh Cb/B falls to the Bb; the chromatic parallelism preserves the interval structure while only the level changes.

transiciones.como: Drop the third D to C and the seventh Ab to Gb, as a block.
transiciones.porque: Both voices fall a whole step and keep the tritone intact, so the dominant color is preserved while the root descends a whole step toward the bVI.

transiciones.como: Raise the fifth E to F and the root A to G#.
transiciones.porque: The F is the dominant's b9 and appears through ascending half-step motion; the G# enters as the third and creates the A–G# chromaticism that announces the return to the i.

transiciones.como: Drop the seventh Eb to D and let the G ring as a ninth turned sixth.
transiciones.porque: The Eb resolves down a half step to the third of the I, and the G shifts from the ninth of the V to the sixth of the I without moving, which smooths the join between the two chords.

transiciones.como: Drop all four voices a half step without changing the fingering.
transiciones.porque: All the tensions move in parallel and the tritone descends a half step, so the arrival at the V is heard as chromatic push rather than a change of function.

transiciones.como: Hold the Eb as the top note and drop the G to F in the bass.
transiciones.porque: The Eb of the i7 is the ninth of the F if you sustain it, and the descending fifth in the bass leaves three notes in common between the two chords.

transiciones.como: Drop the root and seventh by a half step and sustain the Bb as a ninth.
transiciones.porque: The Db falls to C and the Cb falls to Bb, which becomes the ninth of the final chord; two descending half steps are enough to close the cadence.

licks.nota: The lick everyone learns first. The bend at fret 8 on the first string rises a whole step to the tonic.
The blue note is fret 8 on the third string (Eb). Pass through it quickly, don't linger.

licks.nombre: A box with a blue note
licks.nota: Rises D-Eb-E on the third string: the Eb is the flat fifth, the blue note, and it's crossed quickly because its job is to brush the fifth, not settle there. Closes on the tonic.
Classic box with the D bend going up a whole step to E: it's the call gesture that later gets answered in the low register. Everything stays in the same position.
F-F#-G on the third string: the flat fifth appears between the fourth and the fifth and builds the chromatic slide that defines the blues scale.
Drops from the high Bb down to the tonic across the box: it works as an answer to an ascending phrase because it inverts the contour and ends low.
The C-C# step is the heart of the matter: it brushes the minor third and resolves it to the major, which is what makes it sound like blues over a major chord without leaving the chord.
G-G#-A on the third string builds the chromatic climb and then jumps to the high box to close on the tonic: a typical phrase for the last two bars.

The notes cluster on the fourth and the minor seventh, the degrees that define the pentatonic color. The bend on the minor third pulls it toward the major third and creates the typical blues ambiguity.
The A–Bb–B run covers the diminished fifth between the fourth and fifth, the note that separates the blues scale from the pentatonic. Resolving from Bb to B by half step releases that tension.
The line climbs by step and leans on the minor seventh and the fourth, the notes that support the I7. The natural F avoids the major color and keeps the dominant function.

The Bb–B–C stretch chains the two sevenths and lands on the root on a strong beat. That chromaticism is what lets you run eight straight notes without any of them falling outside the chord on the strong beats.

The descent passes through the major sixth and minor seventh, the pair that defines dorian over a ii7. Each note is a step away from the next, so the line reads as voice leading rather than an arpeggio.

The slur between the minor third and the major third is the axis of the scale: two notes a half step apart working as a grace note. The major sixth closes the phrase over the fifth without touching the seventh.
The F–F#–G slur crosses the diminished fifth and leaves it as a passing note between the fourth and the fifth. Ending on the root an octave up closes the line with no ambiguity.
The phrase descends two notes per string, and each pair forms a minor third or a whole step. The opening bend on the minor third rises toward the fourth and gives momentum to the whole descent.

metal.resumen: Phrygian, tritones, and the low sixth string. The tension doesn't resolve: it holds.

progresiones.nota: The phrygian leap. A half step above the tonic: it's the shortest and most uncomfortable distance there is, and it's where the whole genre comes from.
The epic descent. Works as a chorus when the riff needs to open up.
The direct tritone. Unprepared, unresolved.
A closed aeolian cycle: the bVI and bVII are major and rise by step up to the minor tonic. It's the most-used loop in melodic-metal verses.
Andalusian descent with the major V taken from harmonic minor: the borrowed G# adds the half step that restarts the cycle with tension.
Harmonic-minor progression: the bII and the major V share notes and chain two tensions in a row before returning to the tonic.
Pure tritone in power chords: the three-whole-step distance belongs to no stable key, so the passing chord is dissonant by definition. Played with palm mute.
Natural aeolian degrees arranged so the bass moves by fourths and thirds. The final iv darkens it and keeps the loop from sounding resolved.
Combines the aeolian color of the bVI with the phrygian bII: the jump between the two over a tonic pedal keeps the tonal center while the harmony shifts.
The b9 sits a half step from the tonic, and the four upper notes of the chord form a diminished chord: maximum tension with minimum movement.
A chromatic riff in power chords: there's no harmonic function, the logic is displacement by half steps. It works because power chords have no third to define the mode.
Descends through aeolian and ends on the phrygian bII, a half step above the tonic: the cut is abrupt and works as a section-ending.

The bVI shares two notes with the i and its root sits a major third below, so the change happens by moving a single voice. The iv brings back the fourth as the bass and sets up the return via fifth motion.
A riff built on whole tones: every root is a whole step apart and none defines a third, so there's no key. The tritone between the first and last root closes the cycle without resolution.

With the root sounding as a pedal below, the bII5 produces a half step against the pedal and is the point of maximum tension. The bVII5 releases it by dropping a whole step and leaving a seventh interval against the pedal.
The diminished triad over the bVI brings a tritone that doesn't exist in natural minor and pushes toward the bII. From bII to i the root drops a half step, the shortest possible motion to the tonic.
The three degrees come from the minor pentatonic, and the roots move by minor third and whole step. With no thirds in the chords, the weight sits in the interval between roots.
A cycle with no dominant: the bVII and bVI sit a whole step and a step-and-a-half from the i and share notes with it. Ending on bVII leaves the phrase open, since its third doesn't lead to the tonic.

The b9 of the dominant is the same note as the root of the bVI, so moving between those two chords doesn't move the top voice. The seventh of the V falls a half step to the third of the i when the cadence finally resolves.
The roots trace the locrian tetrachord, including its diminished fifth. The absence of a perfect fifth over the tonic is what blocks any sense of rest.

The four roots form a chain of descending fifths except for the first leap, and each chord shares two notes with the next. At a slow tempo, that chain of shared notes sustains the motion with no dominant needed.
The bII and the VII surround the tonic by a half step from above and below. That chromatic pincer is what produces the tension, since neither note belongs to natural minor.

The augmented triad over the bIII appears by raising the seventh of the scale: its G# is the leading tone and rises a half step to the root of the i or to the third of the V7. The two central chords share the C.

The #IV sits a tritone from the tonic, the farthest interval in the cycle, and returning to it sounds like a drop. The final bII leaves the phrase a half step from the tonic and forces the cycle to repeat.

The roots form a diminished arpeggio: every leap is a minor third, and the pattern repeats every three semitones. That symmetry lets you start the riff on any of the four notes without changing the color.

The sus4 delays the third and drops a half step to the minor third on resolution, the gesture that defines the key. Then bVI and bVII rise and fall a whole step while keeping the root of the i as a common note.

The first half moves by thirds and fifths within natural minor; the second introduces the leading tone in the V7 to close. The third D# of the dominant is the only note outside the scale, and it rises a half step to the E.

transiciones.porque: It's the signature of the style. Play the two power chords with the same shape moved up one fret: the physical motion is the sound.
Returns to the tonic without a leading tone. Heavier than a V-i because it doesn't announce itself.
Splits the octave right down the middle. It belongs to no key, which is why it sounds like a threat.
The bass falls a half step to the tonic. It's the shortest possible motion, which is why it sounds heavy and final, with no dominant needed.
