Two major chords a whole step apart push toward the minor tonic without using the dominant's half step. It gives momentum without making the progression tonal.
The mode's major seventh resolves to the tonic, and the b9 falls a half step to the fifth. Two half steps at once: the resolution is immediate.
Holding the tonic open while the harmony moves above generates dissonance on its own: the bVI against the pedal leaves a second that tenses without moving the bass.
Inserting a chord a half step below the target reinforces the arrival by proximity rather than function. It's the logic behind chromatic riffs.
Rises a fourth while keeping the minor mode. No new notes, so it shifts sections without losing the dark color.
They share two notes, and the tonic's minor third becomes the root. The chorus sounds wider without leaving the key.

transiciones.como: Hold the G and drop the E to Eb with the bass on C.
transiciones.porque: The G is a common note between the two triads, and the E–Eb half-step drop creates the C–Gb tritone once the bass enters, which generates the tension.

transiciones.como: Move the power-chord shape a half step up and let the open sixth string ring as a pedal.
transiciones.porque: The root G sits a half step from the F# pedal and its fifth D forms a sixth with it, so the clash concentrates on a single interval.

transiciones.como: Jump the shape six frets up on the same string.
transiciones.porque: Six semitones is the tritone: the fifth of the first chord ends up a half step from the root of the second, with no note in common between the two.

transiciones.como: Raise the G to G# and leave A and C where they are.
transiciones.porque: A single ascending half step turns the minor into augmented and produces the leading tone; A and C remain common notes, so the change is felt as coloring rather than a new chord.

transiciones.como: Keep the F on top and drop the rest to the major-triad voicing.
transiciones.porque: The dominant's b9 is the root of the bVI, so that voice doesn't move; the G# drops to A and the D drops to C, two descending half steps.

transiciones.como: Drop the B to A without touching the root or the fifth.
transiciones.porque: The fourth resolves a half step down to the minor third, the motion that defines the key; with the other voices staying put, the attention lands on that single note.

transiciones.como: Keep D and F and drop the bass to Bb.
transiciones.porque: The bVI contains the root and third of the i, so two of three voices stay fixed and the change happens only in the bass, by descending third.

transiciones.como: Cross to the next string keeping the same relative fret, six semitones up.
transiciones.porque: The diminished fifth between the roots has no implied resolution, which lets the two chords alternate indefinitely with neither functioning as tonic.

transiciones.como: Hold G and Bb and drop the bass a major third.
transiciones.porque: The two upper voices are the third and fifth of the bVI, so only the root moves; at a slow tempo that keeps the harmonic continuity.

transiciones.como: Drop the shape a half step at the end of the phrase.
transiciones.porque: The root ends up a half step below the tonic and functions as a leading tone with no third, forcing the return to i by ascending half-step motion.

licks.nota: Tonic and b2 on the low string, with palm mute. The same shape moved up one fret.
Fret 6 on the sixth string is the b5 (Bb). Go in and out fast: it's a hit, not a place to stay.

licks.nombre: Phrygian riff in E with palm mute
licks.nota: All on the sixth string: the F at the first fret is the minor second, and alternating it with the open tonic is what produces the phrygian rub. Downstrokes with palm mute.
Three hits on the open tonic, the gallop figure, then a G-F# turn and a leap to A-B. The minor seventh and major sixth give it that epic feel.

licks.nombre: Riff in A phrygian, fifth position
licks.nota: Alternates the tonic with the Bb, the minor second, then climbs to E-F on the fifth string: the same half step repeated in another octave reinforces the mode's color.
Climbs the scale up to the G#, the major seventh, which resolves to the tonic a half step up. The F-G# leap is an augmented second, which is what makes it sound neoclassical.
The Bb at the sixth fret is the flat fifth: alternating it with the open tonic leaves the tritone exposed. It ends descending A-G-F to land on the minor second.
The open fourth string works as a pedal, and between hits come Eb, F, and G: the fixed note makes everything else sound like tension against the tonic.
The half step between root and minor second appears in the first two notes and marks the mode right from the start. The rest ascends by step up to the octave without touching any altered note.

The minor second and major third form a minor third interval between each other, and that leap is what sets this mode apart from phrygian. The major third makes it compatible with a dominant chord over the tonic.

The final G#–A stretch resolves the leading tone to the tonic by half step. Between the minor sixth and major seventh there's an augmented second, the step-and-a-half leap that characterizes the scale.
The diminished fifth sits in the middle of the phrase and never resolves upward, so the tonic never gets affirmed. The opening minor second reinforces the instability from the very first interval.
Every interval is a whole step, so there are no half steps to orient the ear toward a tonic. Reaching the octave after six equal steps closes the phrase by symmetry rather than resolution.
The pattern alternates half step and whole step, so each pair of notes repeats the same shape a minor third higher. That lets you move the phrase in three-fret blocks without leaving the scale.

With no seconds or sixths, every interval is a whole step or minor third, and the phrase never brushes a half step. The bend on the fourth pushes it toward the fifth, the only stable support in the scale besides the tonic.
The minor sixth and minor seventh sit a whole step apart and avoid any leading tone, so the tonic holds by repetition rather than attraction. The phrase rises by step up to the octave.

country.resumen: Major and bright, with bends that imitate the pedal steel and basses that walk between chords.

progresiones.nota: The skeleton. What makes it country isn't the chords but how you get to them: by walking the bass.
With the V before the IV, which gives it that honky-tonk sway.
The ballad. The vi opens up space for the sad lyric.
The three basic chords in the most direct order. In country the interest isn't the harmony but what the bass does between chords.
Returns to the tonic before the dominant, so the verse breathes twice on the I. The final V is left open to repeat.
A cycle of fourths typical of western swing: each chord is a fourth above the last, giving constant motion for improvising over the changes.
Turning the tonic into a dominant before the IV adds the minor seventh, which resolves down a half step to the third of the IV. It's the classic push to the fourth degree.
The II7 is the dominant of the dominant: it brings a major third foreign to the key and chains two dominants in a row, that honky-tonk bar sound.
Swing cadence: the I6 in place of the plain triad adds the sixth, softening the close — the typical voicing of western swing guitars.
The bass walks by step instead of leaping between roots: the slash chord lets the bass move without changing the harmony.
A mixolydian borrowing very common in country rock: the bVII replaces the dominant, leaving the progression without a half-step resolution, more relaxed.
A full chain of secondary dominants: each chord sets up the next. Works as a long turnaround at the end of the verse.
The same three functions with extended voicings: sixths and ninths instead of triads. It's the color of western-swing orchestras, more jazz than folk.

The iii shares its third and fifth with the I, so the bass rises a major third without moving the inner voices. The sus4 delays the third of the V for a beat, and the 4–3 resolution lands right before returning to the I.

The IV and the ii7 share three notes, so the move between them feels more like a bass change than a chord change. The seventh of the ii7 falls a half step to the third of the V7, and the circle closes on its own.
The third of the V is the root of the vi, so the V–vi motion turns a common note into a root. The final IV leaves the sixth of the key in the bass of the previous chord, resolved downward by a third.

Starting on IV puts the tonic on the fifth of the chord, leaving the resolution pending until the third bar. The final vi is the relative minor of the I: a single voice changes and the cycle can repeat without a cadence.

The minor seventh added to the I turns it into the dominant of the IV and falls a half step to the third of that chord. The borrowed iv lowers the major sixth of the key to a minor sixth, and that note pushes by half step toward the fifth of the I when it returns.

The bIII brings the key's minor third as its root and deliberately clashes with the major third of the I. Its fifth is the root of the IV, so the link resolves by common note and the bass rises by a whole step.

The I6 and the vi7 have the same four notes: only which one sits in the bass changes. From there the descending circle of fifths chains sevenths falling by half step, and the thirteenth of the V adds the key's third above the dominant.

The major seventh of the I sustains as the fifth of the vi7, so the top voice stays still across two chords. The 6/9 over the IV avoids the seventh and keeps the sound open until the ninth of the V calls for the return to I.

Each chord is the dominant of the next, and the sevenths fall by half step in a chain down to the third of the following chord. Since they're all major, each root brings in a note foreign to the key, justified by the immediate resolution.
The chromatic diminished chord places its root a half step below the ii7 and pushes the bass upward. Its notes are all minor thirds apart, so it works as a passing dominant with no key of its own.
The bVII lowers the key's seventh by a half step and creates a mixolydian modal turn. Its third is the root of the IV, which is why the bVII–IV–I descent sounds like a chain of falling fifths.

The bVII appears after the V, so the leading tone is heard first and then cancelled by a half step. The bass falls by whole step and by fourth, and the final IV becomes a suspended rest instead of a cadence.

With no thirds, the three chords are just root and fifth, leaving the progression ambiguous between major and minor. The motion is parallel by fourths, so the voice leading is a block shift rather than a true connection.

transiciones.porque: Instead of leaping, you walk the in-between notes on the low strings. The listener arrives at the chord before you do.
Resolve by playing two strings at once a third or a sixth apart: it's the sound of two guitars, or of the pedal steel.
Stretch the second up to the major third while holding another string fixed. It imitates the pedal.
Climbing from the I to the IV through the in-between notes fills the bar and announces the change before it arrives. The chord doesn't change until the walk is complete.
The minor seventh added to the tonic resolves down a half step to the third of the IV. It turns a neutral arrival into a resolution.
Playing the third and sixth of the chord together doubles the voice leading: two lines resolving in parallel sound like a two-guitar section.
Each dominant resolves to the next by fourths, so the ear always has somewhere to go. It's what keeps the swing moving.
The plagal close has no tension of its own, so it gets filled with a double-stop lick: the interest comes from the line, not the harmony.
They share two notes, so the bridge shifts mood without modulating. The bass drops a third and the section turns more introspective.
Bending the fourth up to the fifth while another fixed note rings imitates the pedal-steel effect: one voice moves while the other stays still.
The bass rises a whole step instead of a half step. It closes without the formality of the V7, which is why it sounds more countrified and less like a parlor cadence.

transiciones.como: On the last beat of the V7, put the third of the chord in the bass and rise a half step to the root of the iii.
transiciones.porque: The third of the V7 is the seventh of the iii, so the change happens through a common note and only the bass moves.

transiciones.como: Over the IV, add the key's root in the top voice and drop it a half step when the iv comes in.
transiciones.porque: That note is the fifth of the IV and becomes the minor third of the iv, so the passage is defined by a single half step.

transiciones.como: Replace the final V with the III7 and enter the dominant chain from there.
transiciones.porque: The III7 and the V share the key's fifth, and the new seventh of the III7 falls by half step to the third of the VI7.

transiciones.como: Hold the sixth of the I6 and raise it a half step to turn it into a major seventh.
transiciones.porque: The two progressions share the vi7, so the only voice that changes is the one that defines the quality of the first chord.

transiciones.como: Instead of returning to the I after the bVII, raise the bass a minor third from the tonic to the bIII.
transiciones.porque: The bVII and the bIII share two notes, and the minor third that the bIII brings was already present as the seventh of the bVII.

transiciones.como: Remove the thirds from the three chords and keep only root and fifth.
transiciones.porque: With no third, the chords lose function and the progression reads as parallel fifth motion.

transiciones.como: Instead of the chromatic diminished chord, drop the root a minor third to the vi7 and add the sixth to the I.
transiciones.porque: The I6 already contains the four notes of the vi7, so the substitution moves no inner voice.

transiciones.como: From the vi, drop the root a whole step to the V and continue the descent to the bVII.
transiciones.porque: The vi and V share the key's seventh as a common note, and from the V the bVII cancels that same note by a half step.

transiciones.como: Swap the bIII for the V while keeping the key's fifth, which is in both chords.
transiciones.porque: The bIII uses the minor third and the V the leading tone: substituting one for the other moves a single voice a half step in each direction.

transiciones.como: Drop the ninth of the V and lower the major seventh of the I to the sixth and then to the fifth.
transiciones.porque: The IV6/9 and the ii7 share the root and fifth of the IV, so reducing to four-note chords doesn't break the bass line.

licks.nota: Thirds over the tonic. Play both strings together — it's the sound of two guitars.
The notes that connect one chord to the next, on the low strings. Ends on the C of the arriving chord.
Climbs D-E-G-A-B and comes back down the same way, all in third position. The sound comes from the right hand: note muted with the palm, then plucked with the finger.
The bend from E to F# on the second string, with the neighboring notes held still, imitates the steel's pedal: one voice rises while the others sustain the chord.
An ascending run across four strings starting from the open sixth: it works as an intro because it builds up range as it climbs to the chord.
Rises by step from the open fourth string up to the D on the second: the natural C, the minor seventh, is what takes the formality out of the run.

licks.nombre: Honky-tonk in C with a bend
licks.nota: The bend rises a whole step from G to A, and then the phrase falls into the box at the octave position. The pull-off at the end gives the style's typical irregular attack.
Includes the natural F, the minor seventh, which is what makes the phrase sound over a G7 rather than a G major. Ends with a pull-off to slur the finish.

licks.nombre: Pentatonic run on the third string
licks.nota: The phrase chains major and minor thirds of the pentatonic without touching the fourth or seventh, so no degree demands resolution. The final leap of a minor sixth between strings leaves the fifth of the chord on top.

The ascent passes through the minor seventh and the major third in the same phrase, the pair of intervals that defines the dominant. The major sixth enters as a stepwise passing note, avoiding a direct tritone leap.
The line rises by step and uses the fourth as a grace note that falls to the third. The major seventh appears just before the tonic, so the final half step defines the rest.

The chromatic stretch between the major second and the major third passes through the minor third, which works as a passing note rather than a stable degree. Ending on the major sixth leaves the phrase open toward the dominant.
Each string contributes two notes a whole step apart, spreading the scale into major seconds and avoiding consecutive half steps. The major sixth is what sets this passage apart from a natural minor.

licks.nombre: Major bebop with a passing minor fifth
licks.nota: The minor sixth is inserted between the fifth and the major sixth, making the stretch chromatic while the stable degrees fall on strong beats. The major seventh is saved for the final note and closes the half step to the tonic.

The open strings duplicate scale degrees in another octave, so the line alternates registers without changing position. With no fourth or seventh, any order of the notes still sounds consonant over the tonic chord.

The phrase climbs from the fourth up to the major second of the next octave, passing through the major third and the minor seventh. That pair of notes is the dominant chord's tritone, and it's what gives the push.

western.resumen: Harmonic minor, tremolo, and spring reverb. The desert before the duel.

progresiones.nota: The Morricone loop. That A7 with the leading tone comes from harmonic minor and is what puts the danger in it.
Phrygian pendulum. It doesn't go anywhere: it sways, and that stillness is the tension.
The full tragic cadence.
The bVI and V7 sit a half step apart: that falling bass move is the gesture that defines the sound. The V7 brings the major seventh borrowed from harmonic minor.
A cadence stripped to the bare minimum. Used as a song ending because it concentrates all the tension in the descending half step of the bass.
Full andalusian descent: three aeolian degrees falling and the major V at the end. The G# of the dominant against the previous natural G gives the characteristic contrast.
Two-chord pendulum: it alternates tension and rest without moving forward. With no third chord, the feeling is one of waiting, exactly what's wanted in suspense passages.
Phrygian sway: the bII, a half step from the tonic, goes on and off. There's no progression, just a rub, and that's enough to carry a whole section.
Rises by thirds up to the bVI and falls to the V7. The first half sounds major and the second shuts the door with the dominant: the shift in light is the whole device.
The b9 sits a half step from the tonic and sounds diminished; then the bVI opens up the register. The cycle alternates anguish and breadth.
A descending line over a fixed bass: the top voice falls by half steps while the tonic stays still. Each step changes the color without changing the chord.
The bII between the bVI and the V7 adds a second tension: two foreign chords in a row before the dominant make the final resolution weigh more.

The bVI and the iv share two notes, so the bass drops a major third with minimal voice leading. From the bVI the root falls a half step to that of the V7, and the leading tone closes the half step to the tonic.

Placing the bVI before the iv leaves the minor sixth in the bass and delays the subdominant. The seventh of the V7 falls a half step to the third of the i and the leading tone rises, so the cadence closes with two opposing half steps.

The three chords rise by step and none brings a leading tone, so the arrival at the i is modal rather than cadential. The bVII contains the minor seventh, which rises a whole step to the tonic instead of a half step.

The augmented chord is the minor-third triad with its fifth raised a half step, and that note is the key's leading tone. Being built of stacked major thirds, it defines no root, which is why it can land on either the iv or the V7.
The bass descends by step while the upper voices stay fixed on the notes of the i. Each bass note becomes seventh, fifth, and then root in turn, so the same chord changes function three times.

Two chords, major and minor, a whole step apart, with no leading tone and no cadence: the repetition sustains the pulse instead of resolving. The minor third of the i falls a half step to the seventh of the bVII and rises again.
The iv and the bVI share third and fifth, so the opening is a bass change over the same sonority. The bVI–V7 step drops the root by a half step, the strongest motion in the whole progression.

The major seventh of the bII is the key's leading tone, so that chord already contains the note that pushes toward the i. Its root sits a half step above the tonic and a fourth above that of the V7, allowing both resolutions.

The sixth of the iv is the key's leading tone anticipated inside a minor chord. The augmented ninth of the V7 is enharmonic with the minor third of the i, so the dominant chord already carries the minor color of the resolution.

The bVII and bVI alternate a whole step apart and neither contains a leading tone, so the block can repeat without asking for closure. All three chords come from natural minor and share at least one note in pairs.

The bIII is the relative major and shares two notes with the i, so the progression starts with just one voice moving. Then the bass rises by seconds and thirds up to the V7, whose leading tone is the only note outside natural minor.
The ii of harmonic minor is half-diminished because its fifth is the key's minor sixth. That same note reappears as the b13 of the V7 and falls a half step to the fifth of the i.
The roots fall by whole step, whole step, and half step, and each chord keeps the structure of a dominant seventh. The tritones shift in parallel, so none resolves until the V7 reaches the tonic.
With no thirds, only root and fifth remain, so the sonority is just the bass line and nothing else. The minor-sixth–minor-seventh–tonic profile defines the mode even without a single complete chord.

A descending circle of fifths within natural minor, so each seventh falls by half step to the third of the next chord. The V7 breaks the series by raising the leading tone and cutting off the descent.

transiciones.porque: From Bb to A7 drops a half step. It's the fuse: the V7 is already loaded and just needs to fall.
The C# of the A7 pushes toward D. That note isn't in natural minor: that's why harmonic minor is used.
A direct, unprepared leap, like a gunshot. Works to cut the phrase off cold.
The root falls a half step and the chord shifts from rest to maximum tension. It's the style's most recognizable move and works even with no tonic afterward.
The dominant's major seventh resolves up a half step to the tonic. That note doesn't exist in natural minor, and it's what makes the close sound ancient and final.
They share two notes, so the change doesn't modulate — it just widens the range. Works to move from a tense passage into a landscape one.
Repeating tension and rest with no new chords freezes the harmony. It leaves the feeling that something is about to happen and never does.
The bass falls a half step to the tonic with no dominant. With no tritone, the close sounds harsh rather than resolved.
The chord's four upper notes form a diminished chord, and the b9 sits a half step from the tonic: two voices resolve by half step at once.
Rises a fourth while keeping the minor third. No new notes, so it darkens the passage without leaving the key.
The tonic's minor third becomes the root and the color suddenly brightens. Used for the main themes, before returning to minor.

transiciones.como: Instead of going to the iv, drop the root a whole step and add a minor seventh to build the bVII7.
transiciones.porque: The iv and the bVII7 share two notes, and the new seventh sets up the pattern of parallel dominants that keeps descending.

transiciones.como: On reaching the i, return to the bVI while keeping the tonic in the top voice, which is that chord's third.
transiciones.porque: The tonic is a common note between the i and the bVI, so the return doesn't interrupt the top voice and the cycle closes with no cadence.

transiciones.como: Raise the fifth of the bIII a half step before moving to the iv.
transiciones.porque: That fifth becomes the key's leading tone, and the resulting augmented chord already points to the V7 without changing root.

transiciones.como: Strip the thirds from the two chords and add the bVI between the i and the bVII.
transiciones.porque: With only root and fifth left, the contrast lives in the bass, and the bVI completes the half-step descent from the minor seventh.

transiciones.como: Replace the iv with the iim7b5, which is the same chord with its root lowered a minor third.
transiciones.porque: The iim7b5 contains the notes of the iv plus the key's second, and its diminished fifth is the same note that later functions as the b13 of the V7.

transiciones.como: Instead of dropping the bass by step, skip the iv and follow the circle of fifths up to the bVI.
transiciones.porque: Both versions reach the same bVI before the V7, but one moves the bass by seconds and the other by ascending fourths.

transiciones.como: Hold the leading tone brought by the iv6 and use it as the major seventh of the bII.
transiciones.porque: That note is common to both chords, so the fourth-root change doesn't move the top voice.

transiciones.como: Reverse the order of the two middle chords so the bass rises a major third instead of falling.
transiciones.porque: The iv and the bVI share third and fifth, so the swap only changes which note sits in the bass and how it arrives at the V7.

transiciones.como: Jump from the bVII7 to the bIII by dropping the chord's seventh to the third of the next chord.
transiciones.porque: The bVII7 is the dominant of the bIII, and that half-step resolution cuts the chain of parallel dominants at a stable point.

transiciones.como: Leave the final bVI as the starting point and rise to the bVII without returning to the i.
transiciones.porque: The ostinato already contains both chords, so the transition is simply stopping the repeat and closing the ascent by step.

licks.nota: The leap from b6 to 7th (fret 6 to fret 9 on the third string) is the style's signature. Played with tremolo.
Long notes on the low strings, with the spring reverb at maximum.
Circles around the tonic and rises to B and C; the G# on the second string is the major seventh that pushes back to A. Played with tremolo picking, one note at a time.

licks.nombre: Low slide in E harmonic minor
licks.nota: Climbs the two low strings from the open sixth: the final D# is the major seventh, and the slide up to E turns it into an arrival, not just another note.

licks.nombre: Phrase with the major seventh in D
licks.nota: The C# is harmonic minor's major seventh: it appears twice, first as an approach from below and finally hanging a half step from the tonic.
Alternates E and F, the half step that defines the mode, then descends D-C-B to close on the tonic. Played in open position, with steady tremolo and heavy reverb.
Climbs A-Bb-C on the sixth string and continues on the fifth up to the F: the mode's two half steps appear back to back, and the return closes on the tonic.
Has the phrygian bII and the major third at the same time: the F-G# leap is an augmented second and is what sounds like the desert. Closes by descending to the tonic.

licks.nombre: Harmonic minor with an augmented-second leap
licks.nota: The step from the minor sixth to the major seventh is an augmented second, the interval that separates this scale from natural minor. The phrase crosses it twice, so the tension doesn't dissolve even though the contour is ascending.

The minor second and major third coexist in the same phrase, and that half step over the tonic is what forces the dominant sound. The leap from the minor second to the major third opens an augmented second in the low register.

The scale brings a minor second and minor sixth, so there are two half steps pulling downward even though the line rises. The phrase ends on the minor seventh, leaving the whole-step descent to the tonic pending.

Three notes per string in major and minor seconds, with no leading tone, so the octave completes with no pull toward the tonic at all. The half step between the fifth and minor sixth is the only tension point, falling in the middle of the phrase.

licks.nombre: Minor pentatonic with a bend on the seventh
licks.nota: The minor pentatonic leaves out the second and sixth, so the contour stays in fourths and minor thirds with no half steps. The bend raises the fifth toward the minor seventh, the interval that carries the phrase.

licks.nombre: Dorian ascent in the middle register
licks.nota: The major sixth over a minor third is what sets this passage apart from natural minor and removes the half-step drop. The line rises by step and ends on the fourth, left hanging over the tonic chord.

licks.nombre: Harmonic minor toward the leading tone
licks.nota: The phrase rises from the tonic up to the major seventh passing through the minor sixth, so the last stretch is an augmented second followed by a half step. That close leaves the leading tone pointing at the tonic an octave up.

Descending the scale puts the minor second right before the tonic, and that descending half step is the mode's strongest resolution. The minor sixth and major third form an augmented second that appears when crossing strings.

sensual.resumen: Velvet: wide, edgeless chords that stay floating.
sensual.comoUsar: Add the 9th and let the chord ring. Play little and slow: the sensual quality lives in the space you leave, not the notes you add. Avoid the root in the melody — go for the 9th and the 6th, the notes that give it that air.

melancolico.resumen: The nostalgia of what never came back: minor sevenths, no drama.
melancolico.comoUsar: The m7 is the starting point. If you want to tighten the knot, pass a bar through mmaj7: that major seventh inside a minor chord is what hurts. Descending phrases and long notes.

tenso.resumen: Something's about to happen: altered dominants and diminished chords that don't let you breathe.
tenso.comoUsar: Place the altered chord right BEFORE resolving, never on the rest. Tension works if you release it afterward: one tense bar, then resolve on the next. Hold it too long and it stops being tension and becomes noise.

luminoso.resumen: Open sky: major chords with a 9th and that #11 that lifts everything.
luminoso.comoUsar: The key note is the #11 (the raised fourth): it's what turns an ordinary major chord into something cinematic. Let it ring on top, in the highest voice.

oscuro.resumen: Bare, with the flat second: weight, earth, threat.
oscuro.comoUsar: Fewer notes, lower down. Strip the extensions: here the bare chord, or just the fifth alone, weighs more than any color. The b2 is what gives the flavor: use it as the opening note of the phrase.

nostalgico.resumen: An old photograph: major sevenths and sixths, everything rounded off.
nostalgico.comoUsar: The 6th instead of the 7th takes off the jazzy weight and leaves it warmer and older-sounding. Slow arpeggios, no blocked chords.

swing.resumen: Make it walk: dominants with a 13th and bebop chromaticism.
swing.comoUsar: Bebop scales have one extra chromatic note precisely so that, running eighth notes down, the strong beats land on chord tones. Play even eighth notes and let the passing note fall on the weak beat: that's where the swing shows up.

desgarrado.resumen: The wail: the third fighting with itself.
desgarrado.comoUsar: The blues trick is playing the minor third over a chord with a major third: that friction is the wail. Bend the b3 toward the major 3rd without fully getting there, and stay put.

jonico.sabor: The good old major. Sounds like home, like resolved.

lidio.sabor: Major but floating: the #11 gives it that film-score air.

mixolidio.sabor: Major with a minor 7th. It's the scale of the dominant and of rock.

lidioDominante.sabor: Dominant with a #11. Modern jazz, without the rub of the natural 4th.

eolico.sabor: The classic minor, with the flat 6th that makes it melancholic.

dorico.sabor: Minor with a major 6th. Brighter: Santana, funk, modal jazz.

frigio.sabor: Minor with a b2. Spanish, dark flavor, very tense.

frigioDominante.sabor: The flamenco and oriental-metal scale: b2 and major 3rd.

locrio.sabor: The m7b5 scale. Unstable by definition, no rest at all.

menorArmonica.sabor: Minor with a leading tone. The leap from 6th to 7th is its signature.

menorMelodica.sabor: Minor with a major 6th and 7th. Sounds like jazz going up.

alterada.sabor: Every tension altered at once. Maximum pull before resolving.

bebopDominante.sabor: Mixolydian with a passing major 7th. THE sound of swing over a dominant.

bebopMayor.sabor: Major with a passing b6. Swing over major-tonic chords.

bebopMenor.sabor: Dorian with a passing major 3rd. Swing over the minor chords of a ii-V.

bluesMayor.sabor: Major pentatonic plus the brushing b3. Sounds sweet and dirty at once.

pentaMayor.sabor: Five notes, none of them clash. It's the safety net.

pentaMenor.sabor: The blues and rock scale. Direct, no awkward notes.

blues.sabor: Minor pentatonic plus a passing b5. The wail.

tonosEnteros.sabor: Everything a whole step apart: no center, it floats.

disminuidaST.sabor: The same symmetry starting on the half step: it's the one for dominants with a b9. Gives you b9, #9, #11, and 13 without leaving the scale.

intro.lema: The Essence of Sound — by Mau
intro.texto: Progressions, substitutions and licks — with the notes written out, arrows showing where each chord goes, and everything split by color.

estilosVista.intro: Every style has its own thing: what chords it's built from, what scales go on top, its typical transitions and a few licks in tab.
estilosVista.progresionesPista: Play any chord to see it on the fretboard.
estilosVista.licksPista: The number is the fret; the top line is the first string. b = bend, / = slide.

acerca.p1: Each chart shows only the chords that map uses, and in the shape the map itself declares: a star with the tonic at the center, a grid, a converging funnel, a cascade going down in zigzag. If a chord isn't in the drawing, it's because it doesn't belong to that map — which is also why it won't show up as an option to move to.
acerca.p2: Hover over a chord and the rest fades out: only the places you can go from there stay lit up, within this same chart. The list on the right separates what the map proposes (with its own explanation) from the other relationships that exist between those chords, and gives each one its degree — the ii, the V7, the bVI — which is what really orients you.
acerca.p3: Click to lock in a chord and see how to play it: the fingering on guitar and bass, and the keys on piano. The positions are calculated from the chord's notes, aiming to get the root on the bass and keep it within hand reach — the number inside each dot is the degree (1 the root, 3 the third, b7 the minor seventh…).
acerca.p4: Above the chart you can change the tonic: the whole map transposes into that key, chords and notes included, so you're not always practicing in C. And with Circle of fifths you switch to the reference view, where you see the whole system of the 12 keys with this progression lit up on top.
acerca.p5:
This doesn't replace playing and listening — it's a map, not the territory.
        It's there to give you a quick visual reference while you improvise or
        put together a new progression.

aprender.pistaRuta:
Six steps in order. Each one builds on the last, and each one tells you
        when you've got it — not by time, but by what you can do.
aprender.pasarDeEstilo: Moving from one style to another
aprender.pistaPuentes:
Almost everything you know from one style carries over to the next one. This is what
        gets reused and what needs to change.

relacion.dominantizar: turn it into a dominant (same chord with a 7th)
relacion.suDominante: its dominant — the V7 that sets it up

ruta.titulo: The four chords and your ear
ruta.que: Learn a single progression — I–V–vi–IV — in two different keys.
ruta.porque: It's not about playing pop: it's so your hand stops thinking and you can actually listen to what you're doing. Until that's automatic, everything else is just noise.
ruta.listo: You can change chords without looking at your hand while singing over it.

ruta.que: The minor pentatonic in all five positions, in a single key.
ruta.porque: Five notes with nothing that clashes: you can improvise from day one without sounding bad. It's the net that lets you make mistakes.
ruta.listo: You can start a phrase anywhere on the fretboard without searching for it.

ruta.que: The full blues in A, playing both the comping and the solo.
ruta.porque: It's the first format where you comp and solo over the same structure. And it forces you to hear the move to the IV, which is the first transition you have to feel, not count.
ruta.listo: You know what bar you're in without counting.

ruta.titulo: The mode that changes the color
ruta.que: Mixolydian over a dominant, and dorian over a minor.
ruta.porque: Here you stop playing 'the song's scale' and start playing each chord's scale. It's the biggest jump: one different note changes the whole genre.
ruta.donde: Rock (mixolydian) and Blues (dorian over the ii) styles.
ruta.listo: You can hear the difference between mixolydian and ionian without looking.

ruta.que: Identify in each scale which note clashes and where it goes down to.
ruta.porque: It's what separates playing correct notes from playing music. Tension used well is what gives a phrase direction instead of just going in circles.
ruta.donde: Any chord: open the fretboard and pick a scale. The crimson one clashes, the gold one resolves.
ruta.listo: You can put the tense note in on purpose and take it out whenever you want.

ruta.que: Swap a chord for another one that does the same job: tritone sub, relative, borrowed from the parallel.
ruta.porque: It's how you rewrite a progression without breaking it. And it's what lets you put in whatever color you want — sensual, tense, bright — without changing the song.
ruta.donde: Harmonic maps: tritone substitution and modal interchange. And the 'Make it sound…' selector on the fretboard.
ruta.listo: You can take someone else's progression and make it sound like yours.

puentes.comparten: The minor pentatonic and the dominants.
puentes.cambia: Rock hardens the chord (fifths with no third) and adds the bVII from mixolydian. Same solo, different base.

puentes.comparten: The three chords and the form.
puentes.cambia: Country moves to the MAJOR pentatonic and swaps the wail for double-string bends. Same box, three frets up.

puentes.comparten: The fifths and the minor pentatonic.
puentes.cambia: Metal tunes down and replaces the bVII with the phrygian bII. The half-step jump is the whole change.

puentes.comparten: The twelve-bar blues, which in jazz is played the same but with more chords.
puentes.cambia: ii-Vs and bebop scales show up: the same structure with a chromatic passing note.

puentes.comparten: The phrygian mode and unresolved tension.
puentes.cambia: Western swaps distortion for tremolo and reverb, and uses the harmonic minor to get a leading tone. It's the same fear, wearing different clothes.

diccionario.intro: Pick a root and a quality — major, m7, maj9, whatever — and it shows you the notes, the scale-degree formula, and every fingering it finds up and down the whole neck, not just one position.
diccionario.pistaMastil: Each diagram is a different position of the same chord — from open frets all the way up the neck.
diccionario.sinPosiciones: Couldn't find a comfortable fingering for this chord on this instrument.

triadas:.descripcion: The foundation of it all: root, major third, and perfect fifth. Sounds resolved, no tension — the resting point of almost any progression.

triadas:m.descripcion: The third drops a half step and it changes the whole color: from resolved to melancholic. Same fifth as the major, the entire difference is in that third.

triadas:dim.descripcion: Minor third and a lowered fifth too: two minor thirds stacked on top of each other. Unstable by nature — not a chord to sit on, it's a passing chord.

triadas:aug.descripcion: The fifth goes up instead of down. Two major thirds stacked, symmetrical like the diminished but with a different flavor: floating, with no perfect fifth to anchor the chord.

triadas:5.descripcion: Root and fifth, no third. Since it doesn't say whether it's major or minor, it works under any scale on top — that's why it's the backbone of the rock and metal riff.

triadas:sus2.descripcion: The third gets swapped for the second. Leaves an open chord, neither major nor minor, with an airier feel than the sus4.

triadas:sus4.descripcion: The third gets swapped for the fourth, which almost always resolves down to the third. This is the real 'suspense' chord: it asks for resolution.

septimas:7.descripcion: Major triad + minor seventh. The chord of tension that wants to resolve to the tonic — it's the V7 of any key, and the backbone of the blues.

septimas:maj7.descripcion: Major triad + major seventh (a half step below the octave). Sounds like elegant, jazzy rest — it doesn't pull anywhere the way the dominant does.

septimas:m7.descripcion: The everyday minor: it shows up as the ii in any ii-V-I, and as the resting chord in soul and funk progressions.

septimas:m7b5.descripcion: An m7 with a lowered fifth. It's the vii of a major key and the ii of a minor one — almost always passing toward a V7, never a resting chord.

septimas:dim7.descripcion: Symmetrical: the whole chord is minor thirds stacked on top of each other (that 'bb7' sounds like the same key as a 6th, but it's written differently because it plays a different role). Works as a wildcard for moving from one key to another.

septimas:mmaj7.descripcion: Minor third but major seventh: the odd combo used in suspense-film scores and modal jazz. Tense and dark without sounding like a dominant.

sextas:6.descripcion: Like a maj7 but without the jazzy weight: the 6th instead of the major 7th makes it warmer and less 'piano-bar chord.' Common in country and swing.

sextas:m6.descripcion: The minor with that same 6th added. Sounds like old-movie minor — it's the color a dark western reaches for when it doesn't want to go straight to the m7.

sextas:6/9.descripcion: The 6 above with a 9th added on: leaves a wide, tension-free chord, often used to end a song — it resolves without being boring.

extendidas:9.descripcion: A 7 with a 9th on top. Still a dominant (it wants to resolve) but with more color — funk and soul use it constantly.

extendidas:m9.descripcion: An m7 with the 9th added: THE 'sultry' chord of this whole dictionary — wide, no rough edges, nothing that clashes.

extendidas:maj9.descripcion: The everyday maj7 with a 9th on top. It's the 'open sky' sound of a well-dressed major resting chord.

extendidas:11.descripcion: A 9 with the 11th added. In practice the 11th clashes with the major third, so it's almost always played without the 3rd, or the 11th is left to work as a passing color.

extendidas:m11.descripcion: The minor version of the 11: here the 11th doesn't clash with anything (there's no major third to fight it), so it sounds much more natural than the dominant 11.

extendidas:13.descripcion: The most dressed-up dominant: 7 + 9 + 13 (the 11th is almost always left out, for the same friction reason as in the plain 11). Big, big-band and jazz-funk sound.

agregadas:add9.descripcion: A major triad with the 9th added straight in, WITHOUT going through the seventh. Different from a true 9th chord: there's no hidden dominant here, just extra color on a resting major.
